executionWorkflow.inspect: Identify the exact target rig and classify the job as authored clip, playback controller, locomotion, combat, tool alignment, NPC/creature, IK/procedural overlay, face, cinematic or diagnosis. Read the actual joint/bone graph, scale, rest transforms, Humanoid/AnimationController/Animator, Animate script, assets, remotes and competing controllers. Distinguish R6, R15, custom rigid and skinned rigs; never assume human part names on a creature. Record asset ownership/permission and whether the clip is local editable source or a usable published asset. Select the real server/client execution context and exact tool schema; a connection label is not rig inspection.
executionWorkflow.execute: Author/reuse editable clips on the actual rig and keep their source. Integrate with the server-created/replicated Animator after the rig is in Workspace; load through Animator:LoadAnimation and cache tracks per rig lifetime instead of loading on every trigger. Set purposeful priority, loop, weight and fade behavior. Length may be zero while loading, so timing must not assume immediate availability. Track one owner per transform/channel; procedural overlays and IK must respect the animation evaluation phase and current rig APIs. Feature-check modern graph/constraint APIs against the installed Studio documentation before adopting them. Graph parameter names/types come from the actual authored graph; Speed and Grounded are examples, not universal built-ins. Avoid replacing a working Animate/controller just to add one action. Player presentation may start responsively on the owning client using the correctly replicated Animator; non-player animation that must replicate is loaded/started on the server. Verify the actual ownership setup rather than generalizing a solo test. Bind marker signals before playback and use named markers for cosmetic timing. Damage, cooldowns, inventory and hit validation remain server-owned and must not trust a client marker or animation ID. Blend locomotion/actions with explicit entry/exit/interruption rules. Cache and disconnect marker/track signals; distinguish playback stopping from complete fade-out when cleaning up. Cinematics own a cancellation token, saved camera/control state, render binding and one cleanup path for normal finish, error, death, respawn and replacement. Align weapon grips/attachments to the actual hand and rig rather than eyeballing an unrelated asset.
executionWorkflow.verify: Play the real clip/controller at normal and slow speed on the intended rig. Check contacts, arcs, deformation extremes, loop seams, foot sliding, priority/weight transitions and repeated triggers. Exercise locomotion → action → interruption → recovery, equip/unequip, jumping/falling/landing, death/respawn, target destruction and missing/denied assets. Use a multi-client/server test for replication claims and test in the published ownership context when asset permissions matter. Inspect logs, active track/connection counts and repeated NPC density. Capture a short recording or equivalent temporal evidence; a single still frame cannot prove a transition. Report clip source, real IDs, controller paths, ownership decisions, tests and unresolved publishing/device checks separately. Read final source back and use an advertised syntax/analysis tool or an actual Luau compiler when available. Requiring a ModuleScript runs it and is not a compile-only check; unavailable restricted compilation stays explicitly unverified.
executionWorkflow.craft: Plan anticipation, decisive contact/action, follow-through and recovery with clear silhouette at the gameplay camera distance. For locomotion define gait phase, planted contacts, stride/cycle speed and a compatible loop seam. For combat define startup, authoritative active interval, recovery, interruption and return to locomotion. Create a manifest of purpose, rig, actual asset ID or explicit unavailable placeholder, priority, loop, fade/speed, markers and permitted owner. Decide which layer owns movement, pose, camera, audio, VFX and damage. An authored root displacement is not automatically authoritative world travel. Use references for timing, weight and arcs without copying another rig's channels or inventing a published upload. OMNI 6.50: For pose, timing, interruption and UI/VFX/animation event composition, use ms_roblox_omni only when its reference/recipe/native modules help the current task. Query a few relevant entries and retain the existing primary style; source screenshots and approximate tokens are not verified assets or runtime evidence. The reviewed native kit and ms_forge complement existing project components. Apply useful increments through real engine tools, test actual behavior and reuse loaded guidance; no mandatory preparation/progress ritual.

executionWorkflow.handoff: State owned files/assets, adjacent interfaces and acceptance criteria. In co-work, read the board and claim disjoint resources; do not overwrite another worker.

executionWorkflow.recovery: No playback: inspect asset permission, loading errors, Animator ancestry/Workspace presence and rig compatibility. Track time advances but pose does not: inspect actual channels, priority/weight and competing transform writers. Owner sees it but peers do not: verify server-created Animator, correct character/owner, NPC server playback and a real multi-client reproduction. Popping/foot sliding: compare rest pose, loop seam, contacts, movement speed and fades before adding keys. Missing marker: verify exact case/name, signal hookup before playback, loop/retrigger behavior and early stop. IK instability: inspect chain, target/pole reach and blend/cleanup. Cutscene leaves a Scriptable camera: repair the shared exit path. Never bypass restricted capabilities, fabricate IDs or claim that a local KeyframeSequence was published; preserve source and provide an explicit upload/permission handoff.

executionWorkflow.inspect: Survey StarterGui and runtime PlayerGui, existing ScreenGuis/controllers, StarterPlayer scripts, ReplicatedStorage state/remotes and the server handlers for inventory, purchases and rewards. Record the owner, state source, local action, authoritative request, existing token module and objects to preserve for each requested screen. Identify framework/Rojo/generated-source ownership before choosing an edit tool. Do not create a second menu, competing controller or duplicate remote just because inspection returned an incomplete page. Confirm a specific target path and reuse valid results until the project changes.
executionWorkflow.execute: Use ScreenGui for the screen root and native layout objects for managed lists/grids. Mix scale for relationships with offset for padding and legible detail; apply AnchorPoint and sensible size/aspect constraints. Give each layout property one owner: do not overwrite UIListLayout/UIGridLayout positioning in a frame loop. Use readable TextSize with wrapping/content growth where appropriate; bound deliberate TextScaled usage instead of combining competing sizing rules. Choose ScreenInsets for actual interactive safe areas rather than blindly disabling insets. Use verified image IDs and intentional tile/slice scale; layered frames can express depth without inventing CSS blur or box-shadow APIs. Build reusable controls with an accessible hit area even when the visible glyph is small. Connect Activated through the existing controller and trace input → validation → state → visual feedback for every visible action. A shop must use real item definitions, authoritative price/balance/result and pending/refused/retry states; a decorative purchase button is unfinished. Inventory needs stable item keys, selection, filter/sort, empty state and authorized equip/use actions. HUD values come from actual state events. Local presentation may predict feedback but cannot grant currency, purchases or damage. Maintain one modal/navigation state, focus capture/return, back/cancel and input-lock ownership. Cancel/retarget old tweens and guard completion with a transition generation so a stale close cannot hide a reopened screen. Initialize idempotently and tear down signals, render bindings, temporary instances and input locks on destroy/respawn.

Compare an actual capture against the token sheet and observed references; a hierarchy dump does not verify appearance. Inspect output and listener/instance growth after repeated use. Plan normal, focused, pressed, disabled, pending, empty, error and success states. For each reference record its source, observed proportions and the principle being adapted. Inspect the image rather than inventing details from a search snippet. Studded is a restrained raised-brick material language; cartoon uses readable exaggerated forms; tactical uses disciplined hierarchy. Preserve the existing visual vocabulary unless replacement was requested. Decide how the screen adapts to touch/gamepad, safe areas and long localized content before adding ornament. executionWorkflow.recovery: Find the failed layer before redesigning. Invisible GUI: check correct StarterGui/runtime PlayerGui owner, Enabled/Visible, LocalScript startup and errors. Dead/double buttons: check the actual Activated target, duplicate initialization and in-flight ownership. Phone clipping: inspect anchors, content growth, constraints and safe insets; don't shrink all labels. Jitter: check layout/tween competition and stale callbacks. A closed panel blocking gameplay: release its backdrop, focus and input lock. Missing icons: verify asset permission/ID and show a usable fallback. check-clean-ui.name: Check-Clean-UI - build any Roblox UI, any style
check-clean-ui.description: Always use for Roblox UI. Builds any UI in any style (cartoon is the default), with a design system, layout and responsive rules, component recipes, StyleSheet, gamepad and accessibility rules, and a performance section. The checks are internal; the user gets a short plain summary. Also covers studded, skeuomorphic, steampunk, comic, clay, neumorphic, neubrutalist, Y2K, pixel, paper, terminal, holographic, aurora, low-poly, bento and gacha looks, plus UI techniques, widgets and inventory rules. Also builds 3D models from Parts or toolbox assets and shows them in the UI with ViewportFrames (item, pet and character previews), and the studded simulator shop look. Finds good pictures by searching the Creator Store with several phrasings, looking at real thumbnails and checking the finished screen. Screens are finished only when full, measured for contrast, fitted and reviewed; includes a candy and sweets style.
steps: Mandatory standard for building ANY Roblox UI in any style: menus, HUDs, shops, inventories, dialogue, quest logs, settings, leaderboards, notifications, loading screens, minimaps, billboards and on-part screens. Built from the official Roblox UI docs (containers, layout, constraints, appearance modifiers, styling, input, gamepad, accessibility) plus community UI practice. The checks are internal; the player gets a short plain summary.

Keep this standard to yourself. Do not name the skill, its rules, check codes, colour values or asset ids to the user unless they ask. Apply it silently and tell them about the result, not the method.

Core: Style first. If the user names a style or a mood (sleek, modern, horror, sci-fi, fantasy, minimal, retro, pixel, realistic, tactical, glass, dark, pastel, anything else), build that, using its style section as a starting point and the user's words as the final say. If they show an existing UI in the project, match it. If they name nothing, use the Cartoon style. Never mix two style families in one screen.

Core: Plan before building: the screen's one main job, the one action that matters most, and what the player must see at a glance. Then pick the style, then the devices (phone, tablet, desktop, console) and build for all of them from the start.

Core: Structure: one `ScreenGui` per screen group with `ResetOnSpawn = false`, `ZIndexBehavior = Enum.ZIndexBehavior.Sibling`, a sensible `DisplayOrder`, then a `Root` frame, then Header, Body and Footer frames. Name every instance for what it is (`BuyButton`, not `Frame2`). Set properties first and `.Parent` last. UI scripts are LocalScripts on the client; the server validates every purchase, equip, claim or other action the UI asks for.

Core: Sizes: use Scale for layout and Offset only for borders, padding, icons and fixed-size controls. Add a `UIAspectRatioConstraint` to anything that must stay square or a set ratio, a `UISizeConstraint` for min and max size, and a `UITextSizeConstraint` when text uses `TextScaled`. Let layout objects position things (`UIListLayout`, `UIGridLayout`, `UIPageLayout`, `UITableLayout`, `UIPadding`); do not hand-place rows. Use `AutomaticSize` for content-driven sizes and `ScrollingFrame.AutomaticCanvasSize` for lists.

Core: Layout objects control Position and Size of their children, so a Tween on a child's Position inside a layout is overridden. Animate an inner wrapper, the child's `UIScale`, transparency or rotation instead. `UIFlexItem` (FlexMode Fill, Grow, Shrink or Custom) inside a `UIListLayout` lets one child take the leftover space.

Core: Clicks: connect `Activated` on buttons. It fires for mouse, touch and gamepad. Hover states use `MouseEnter` and `MouseLeave`, which never fire on touch, so every state change must also work without hover. A full-screen dim `Frame` with `Active = true` stops clicks reaching the game behind a modal.

Core: Do not cover the default Roblox controls: the menu and chat area at the top left, the thumbstick at the bottom left and the jump button at the bottom right on phones. Respect `ScreenGui.ScreenInsets` (`CoreUISafeInsets` is the default; `TopbarSafeInsets` and `DeviceSafeInsets` are the others) rather than hard-coding the top bar height. `IgnoreGuiInset = true` only for full-screen backgrounds.

Core: Replacing a default (backpack, health, player list, chat, emotes): turn it off with `StarterGui:SetCoreGuiEnabled(Enum.CoreGuiType.X, false)` inside a `pcall` retry loop, because it can fail early at startup, and rebuild its behaviour (a custom hotbar reads `Player.Backpack` and equips with `Humanoid:EquipTool`).

Core: Never invent `rbxassetid` numbers. Use an id only if it is in the project, the user gave it, or `search_asset` / the Creator Store returned it and you confirmed it loads. If an image fails, fall back to a plain solid fill, not an empty box.

Core: Check the real result: read properties back from Studio, then capture the screen at a phone size and a desktop size (the Device emulator). Look for clipped or overlapping text, controls under the top bar or thumbs, items too small to tap, low contrast, and anything that overflows. Fix every failure before replying.

Core: Treat these as failures to fix silently: text cut off or overflowing, controls under 40 px on a phone, text under 12 px, two overlapping interactive elements, a window that cannot be closed, a menu that stays open after its action, an empty ScrollingFrame that never shows a scrollbar when content is longer, a button with no pressed or disabled state, UI that only works with a mouse.

Core: UI facts (official): `UIScale` multiplies its parent's size. `UIGradient` affects only its own parent (one per object), is not supported on ScrollingFrame or TextBox, should not sit on text that has a `TextStrokeColor3`, and should keep colour sequences to six stops or fewer; animate `Offset` or `Rotation` instead of re-setting `Color`. `UICorner` cannot be applied to a ScrollingFrame, and a radius above half the shorter side makes a pill. `UIStroke` on text outlines the glyphs unless `ApplyStrokeMode` is `Border`; tweening `Thickness` on text can flicker, so tween the object's scale instead.

Core: Docs (look here before guessing an API; class pages are at https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/<ClassName>): ScreenGui, GuiObject, UIListLayout, UIGridLayout, UIFlexItem, UIPadding, UIAspectRatioConstraint, UISizeConstraint, UITextSizeConstraint, UIScale, UIStroke, UIGradient, UICorner, CanvasGroup, ScrollingFrame, ImageLabel, TextLabel, GuiService, UserInputService, ContextActionService, TweenService, StyleSheet. Guides: https://create.roblox.com/docs/ui and https://create.roblox.com/docs/production/publishing/accessibility

Core: Pictures must be the right pictures and the finished screen must be looked at: search the Creator Store with several phrasings, look at the real thumbnails, reject mismatches, check the picture at its final size, and finish with a screen capture to look for empty boxes, blank or wrong images, clipped or misspelt text and low contrast. Never keep a bad match; draw it from shapes or Parts instead.

Core: A screen is finished only when it is full and checked: every tab and list filled with real entries (never an empty panel), the main button tied to a selected item, contrast measured (4.5:1 text, 3:1 large text and icons, inactive tabs still readable, never same-hue text on its plate), text fitted with no clipping, pictures that match, and a last capture reviewed. Fix every failure before replying.

Core: No emojis in any interface text, ever. Emoji characters render from the player's system font, so they show as empty boxes, change shape between phones, clash with the art style and break text fitting. Do not put them in titles, buttons, tabs, labels, prices, toasts, tooltips, notifications or placeholder text, and never use a special character for a currency, star, heart, lock, arrow or check. Use a real picture of the right thing (verified image asset), a shape drawn from Frames, `UICorner`, `UIStroke` and `UIGradient`, a small 3D model in a `ViewportFrame`, or one icon from the `BuilderIcons` font (`rbxasset://fonts/families/BuilderIcons.json`, monochrome, one size and weight) instead. Text says words; symbols are drawn.

Talking to the player: a short plain message about what you made or changed and where it is in Studio. Add only what needs their action or changes what they see, in everyday words (for example that the look needs their eyes in Studio, or that an image did not load and a plain fill was used). No check tables, codes, rule numbers, colour values, asset ids or instance names unless asked. Never say it works or looks good unless you measured it; the player decides whether the look is right.

Design system: Colour: pick one background family, one surface colour a step lighter, one accent for the main action, one warning colour and one success colour. Roughly 60% background, 30% surfaces, 10% accent. Limit a screen to one accent hue plus neutrals; semantic colours (green good, red danger, amber warning) keep their meaning everywhere.

Design system: Contrast: normal text against its background needs at least 4.5:1, large text (about 24 px, or 19 px bold) and control borders at least 3:1 (WCAG). Light grey on white and mid-grey on dark fail often. Do not rely on colour alone: pair it with an icon, shape or label.

Design system: Type: at most two fonts per game and three sizes per screen: title, body and caption. Titles are about 1.5 to 2 times body size. Body text at 16 px or more on desktop and not under 14 px on phones. Use weight and colour for emphasis before size. Left-align reading text; centre only short labels and numbers.

Design system: Spacing: use a 4/8 px rhythm (4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32). Same padding inside every card, same gap between siblings, bigger gaps between groups than inside them. Related things sit close; unrelated things get air. Never let content touch a panel edge: use `UIPadding`.

Design system: Hierarchy: one focal point per screen (the main button or the key number), clearly bigger or brighter than the rest. Secondary actions are quieter (outline or muted fill). Destructive actions are separated and need a confirm. Show only what the player needs now; put the rest behind tabs, a scroll area or a detail view.

Design system: Shape language: pick one corner radius family for the whole game (square, small 4 to 8 px, large 12 to 20 px, or full pill) and one stroke weight. Icons share one style (all outline or all filled) and one visual size. Alignment grids beat decoration.

Design system: Touch targets: phone buttons at least 44 x 44 px with at least 8 px between neighbours (WCAG 2.2 sets 24 x 24 px as the absolute minimum). Put the primary action where a thumb reaches: lower half, right side. Make the clickable area the whole card, not only the label.

Design system: States: every interactive element has default, hover, pressed, selected (gamepad focus), disabled and, where it applies, loading. Disabled looks clearly inactive and says why when it can ('Need 50 more coins'). Show feedback within 0.1 s of a press.

Design system: Numbers and text: abbreviate big numbers (1.2K, 3.4M, 5.6B) with a helper, keep the full value in a tooltip or detail view; use `TextTruncate = Enum.TextTruncate.AtEnd` on names; keep labels to one to three words; use `RichText` for inline colour or bold. Always leave room for longer text in other languages.

Cartoon style: This is the default look when the user names no style (simulators, tycoons, obbies, clickers) and whenever they ask for cartoon, chunky, cute or colourful. One fixed look: use these recipes exactly. If the user names a different style, none of the Cartoon style rules apply; use that style's section instead and keep the Core and Design system rules.
Cartoon style: Font: every text object uses `Enum.Font.GothamBlack` with a black `UIStroke` of 2.0 to 3.5 px, scaled to the text size.
Cartoon style: Window canvas: solid `Color3.fromRGB(59,88,102)` (#3B5866), `BackgroundTransparency = 0`, `UICorner` 4 px, outer `UIStroke` 3.5 px `(24,30,34)` in Border mode. Never translucent.
Cartoon style: Header: 60 px tall, gradient from the archetype table. Under it a 2-tier divider: a 3 px bar in the archetype's divider-dark colour, then a 3 px solid black bar.
Cartoon style: Damier (checkerboard): `rbxassetid://385956923`, tiled, full height of the header or window, with a vertical `UIGradient` transparency of 1 > 0.82 > 0.35 > 0.10. No hard cutoff line.
Cartoon style: Icons: `ScaleType = Fit`. Never stretched.
Cartoon style: Interactive elements: `AnchorPoint = (0.5,0.5)` and a child `UIScale` named `ButtonScale`, so hover and click scale from the centre.

Cartoon style: Responsive: each window has a `UIScale` named `WindowScale`. Scale = `min(viewport.X/1050, viewport.Y/620)` from `camera.ViewportSize`, clamped to 0.52..1.18. Set it when the window opens and when `ViewportSize` changes.
Cartoon style: Archetypes: build every menu from one of five: Shop, Codes, Rebirth, Settings, Daily Rewards. For any other menu use the nearest one.
Cartoon style: Archetype headers (RGB): | Archetype | Gradient top > bottom | Top highlight | Damier | Divider dark |
Cartoon style: Archetype headers (RGB): | Daily Rewards | (152,255,0) > (80,208,0) | (224,255,176) | (53,128,0) | (37,96,0) |
Cartoon style: Panels: Card background (26,44,52). Card inner stroke (75,125,145), 1.2 px, transparency 0.4.
Cartoon style: Panels: Requirements box (20,34,42) with a 1.2 px stroke (85,140,160).
Cartoon style: Close button: 38x38 `ImageButton`, `AnchorPoint (0.5,0.5)`, position `(1,-34,0.5,-2)` in the header, `BackgroundColor3 (115,0,16)` (this is the bevel), black `UIStroke` 2.8 Border.
Cartoon style: Close button: `Face` Frame, size `(1,0,1,-4)` (so a 4 px bevel shows), gradient rotation 90 from (255,125,175) to (255,20,40).
Cartoon style: Close button: Inner highlight: a transparent Frame inset 1 px each side with a `UIStroke` (255,210,235), 1.2 px.
Cartoon style: Close button: 1 px separator Frame (70,0,10) at the bottom edge of the face.
Cartoon style: Close button: Label `X`, GothamBlack 29, white, black `UIStroke` 3.0, centred on the face.
Cartoon style: Close button: Child `UIScale` named `ButtonScale`.
Cartoon style: Iconless button: Any button without an icon uses this recipe and nothing else. Default size 176x55.
Cartoon style: Iconless button: `ImageButton`, `AnchorPoint (0.5,0.5)`, `ClipsDescendants = true`, `AutoButtonColor = false`. Sharp corners: no `UICorner`.
Cartoon style: Iconless button: `OuterStroke`: 3 px `(12,20,26)`, Border mode.
Cartoon style: Iconless button: `ButtonGradient`: rotation 90. Default (255,232,8) to (255,104,0), or the state colours below.
Cartoon style: Iconless button: `Checkerboard`: ImageLabel `rbxassetid://385956923`, tiled 19x19, black, with a 90 degree gradient transparency 0.91 > 0.62.
Cartoon style: Iconless button: `InnerHighlight1/2/3`: transparent Frames inset 2, 4 and 6 px, each with a white 1 px `UIStroke`, transparency 0.25, 0.45, 0.80.
Cartoon style: Iconless button: `Label`: GothamBlack, white, default size 36, position `(0.5,0,0.5,-1)`, `UIStroke` 3 px `(17,23,26)` in Contextual mode.
Cartoon style: Iconless button: `ButtonScale` UIScale.
Cartoon style: Button state colours (gradient top > bottom, damier colour): | State | Gradient | Damier | Bevel colour | Highlight |
Cartoon style: Button state colours (gradient top > bottom, damier colour): | Claim / Buy / Redeem (lime) | (180,255,25) > (105,225,0) | (40,160,20) | (15,120,15) | (235,255,130) |
Cartoon style: Button state colours (gradient top > bottom, damier colour): | Claimed / Disabled (silver) | (216,222,228) > (148,160,176) | (96,104,112) | (72,82,96) | (255,255,255) |
Cartoon style: Button state colours (gradient top > bottom, damier colour): | Locked / Destructive (red) | (255,32,80) > (208,0,32) | (144,0,24) | (112,0,16) | (255,176,200) |
Cartoon style: Button state colours (gradient top > bottom, damier colour): | Skip (amber) | (255,208,0) > (255,140,0) | (176,96,0) | (153,76,0) | (255,240,160) |
Cartoon style: Button state colours (gradient top > bottom, damier colour): | Music on (pink) | (255,20,128) > (212,0,85) | (160,0,64) | (120,10,45) | (255,176,208) |
Cartoon style: Button state colours (gradient top > bottom, damier colour): A button's state sets its gradient and damier colour. Claim, Claimed and Locked are the three states of one reward button.

Cartoon style: Progress bar: Trough (20,30,36) with a 2 px stroke (12,18,22), clipped. Fill gradient (255,200,0) > (255,106,0) with a 2 px bottom bevel (153,60,0). Label GothamBlack 22, white, stroke 2.6.
Cartoon style: Motion: Hover: `ButtonScale` to 1.05 over 0.08 s, Quad Out. Leave: back to 1.0.
Cartoon style: Motion: Press: 0.94 over 0.05 s. Release: back to hover scale over 0.12 s, Back Out.
Cartoon style: Motion: Sunbursts rotate 20 degrees per second only while their window is visible. Disconnect the update when the window is hidden or destroyed.
Cartoon style: Motion: Assert `AnchorPoint == Vector2.new(0.5,0.5)` before binding animations.

Cartoon style: Assets: Confirm that the damier id and any other `rbxassetid` you use load in this experience. Never invent ids. If one does not load, use a plain solid fill instead. Use `CheckUIIcons` only if that module exists in the project.

Cartoon style: Defaults where the source standard contradicted itself (apply silently): Claim, Skip and the other state buttons follow the iconless recipe (sharp corners, no bevel). The close button keeps its own 4 px bevel. The bevel and highlight colours in the state table are for a beveled variant, used only if the user asks.
Cartoon style: Defaults where the source standard contradicted itself (apply silently): Windows and headers use the 4-point damier fade. Buttons use the 2-point fade (0.91 > 0.62).
Cartoon style: Defaults where the source standard contradicted itself (apply silently): Skip uses the iconless recipe with the amber colours. There is no rounded Skip header button.

Components: Currency and stat bar: icon plus number, number abbreviated, count-up tween on change (0.3 to 0.6 s), a small pop (scale 1.15 and back) on gain. Place in the top corner away from the Roblox menu. Update on the value-changed event, not every frame.

Components: Health, stamina and progress bars: a trough frame (dark), a fill frame sized by Scale on X and tweened (0.15 to 0.3 s), a text readout only when it helps, a colour shift (green, amber, red) at set thresholds, and an optional trailing 'damage' bar that catches up after a short delay. Clip rounded bars with `ClipsDescendants` on the trough. Never size the fill with Offset.

Components: Hotbar and inventory: a `UIGridLayout` of equal slots (slot art through `UIAspectRatioConstraint = 1`), slot number or key hint in a corner, item icon, stack count bottom right, equipped highlight with a stroke or scale, empty slots visibly empty. Drag and drop: lift (scale 1.1, raise `ZIndex`), highlight valid targets, snap or return, and always confirm the swap on the server. Inventories longer than about 40 slots use a ScrollingFrame with pooled slots.

Components: Shop: grid of item cards (art, name, price with currency icon, one buy button). Buy button states: affordable, can't afford (disabled with the shortfall), owned (disabled or 'Equip'), locked (with the unlock condition). Confirm only for expensive or irreversible buys. Robux items call `MarketplaceService:PromptProductPurchase` or `PromptGamePassPurchase`; the server grants the item in `ProcessReceipt`. Read prices with `GetProductInfoAsync` inside a `pcall`.

Components: Dialogue: speaker name, portrait optional, text revealed with `MaxVisibleGraphemes` (tween or step it), click or key to finish the line instantly then to advance, a next indicator, and choice buttons stacked below. Place it low and wide. Never trap the player: always allow skip or close.

Components: Quest log and objective tracker: a list of quests on the left with a detail pane on the right (a single column on phones), progress bars or 'x / y' counters, a reward preview, and a small always-on tracker with one to three lines in a screen corner. Update on progress events and flash the changed line briefly.

Components: Settings: grouped rows of label plus control (toggle, slider, dropdown, keybind), changes applied live, saved per player, and a reset-to-default. Sliders: drag with `UserInputService.InputChanged`, clamp, snap to a step, show the value. Offer volume, graphic quality and a reduce-motion option at least.

Components: Leaderboard and scoreboard: rank, avatar or icon, name, value; highlight the local player's row; sort once when data changes, not each frame; pooled rows for long lists; global boards read an `OrderedDataStore` on a cache of 30 to 60 s so the request budget is not burned.

Components: Toast notifications: stack in a `UIListLayout` in one corner, maximum three visible, queue the rest, slide and fade in over about 0.25 s, auto-dismiss after 3 to 5 s (longer for long text), pause on hover, never block input. Colour and icon show the type (info, success, warning, error).

Components: Modal and confirm dialog: dim backdrop (black at 0.4 to 0.6 transparency, `Active = true`), centred panel, a clear title, one sentence of body, primary action on the right or bottom, cancel as the quieter button, close on Esc or gamepad B, and only one modal at a time. Move gamepad focus into it, then restore focus on close.

Components: Loading screen: a LocalScript in `ReplicatedFirst` calls `ReplicatedFirst:RemoveDefaultLoadingScreen()` as early as possible, shows its own `ScreenGui` (`IgnoreGuiInset = true`), waits for `game:IsLoaded()` and any `ContentProvider:PreloadAsync` list you chose (with a timeout so it can never hang), shows real progress or a calm animation, then fades out and destroys itself. Provide a minimum display time of about one second so it does not flash.

Components: Minimap and compass: a `ViewportFrame` with a top-down camera, or a map `ImageLabel` with dots placed by a world-to-map conversion; clip it with `ClipsDescendants`; update at 10 to 15 Hz, not each frame; rotate with the camera only if the player expects it.

Components: Crafting and upgrades: recipe list, requirement rows coloured have/need (for example 3/5), a craft button disabled until requirements are met, a result preview, and server validation. Show what changes (stat from 10 to 14) next to an upgrade button.

Components: Tooltip: appears after about 0.3 s hover, follows or anchors near the pointer, clamps inside the viewport, never covers the thing it describes, and on touch or gamepad shows on tap or focus (`SelectionGained`), not hover.
Components: Title screen and main menu: big game title, one obvious Play button, a few secondary buttons (Settings, Shop, Credits), a quiet animated background; focus goes to Play for gamepad.

Components: Cooldown and ability buttons: icon, key hint, a radial or vertical fill overlay (`UIGradient` rotation or a shrinking frame) for the cooldown, a number only under 10 s, and a clear ready flash.
Components: Damage numbers, name tags and health bars above heads are `BillboardGui` (see World UI). Keep their number low and set `MaxDistance`.

Sleek modern style: Dark neutral base (18,18,24), panels (28,28,38), borders (255,255,255) at 0.9 transparency, one accent such as indigo (99,102,241) or teal (20,184,166). Text (240,242,248) with a muted secondary (150,156,172). Fonts: `Enum.Font.GothamMedium` or `GothamBold` for titles and `Gotham` for body (or BuilderSans).

Sleek modern style: Corners 8 to 12 px, 1 px strokes, no heavy outlines, no bright gradients (a faint vertical gradient of 4 to 6 percent brightness is enough). Depth from a darker offset frame or a soft slice-image shadow, not black outlines. Generous padding (16 to 24).

Sleek modern style: Motion is small and fast: 0.12 to 0.2 s, Quad or Quart Out; hover brightens 6 to 8 percent; press scales to 0.97. Panels fade and slide 12 to 16 px. Icons are one consistent line weight.

Glass style: Panels use a white or tinted fill at 0.85 to 0.92 transparency with a 1 px white stroke at about 0.7 transparency, a soft top-to-bottom `UIGradient` of transparency, and a large radius (16 to 24 px). Text on glass must still reach 4.5:1: put a darker tint behind it or use a heavier weight.

Glass style: Roblox cannot blur behind a single UI element. The honest way is a `BlurEffect` in `Lighting` that blurs the 3D world while the menu is open (tween `Size` from 0 to about 16 to 24 over 0.25 s on open and back to 0 on close; Gui draws on top, so the UI stays sharp). Do not stack many fake 'blur' frames. Heavier tricks with `EditableImage` are costly and experimental; avoid them unless asked.

Horror style: Near-black (8,8,10) with desaturated bone text (200,195,180) and a single dried-blood accent (150,20,20) used rarely. Sparse HUD: hide what the player does not need, fade stats in only when relevant (low stamina, low battery). Prefer diegetic feedback (flashlight dimming, breathing, heartbeat sound) over bars.

Horror style: Fonts: `Creepster` only for the title; body in `SpecialElite`, `Antique` or `Garamond`. Sharp corners, thin worn strokes, a low-opacity noise or vignette overlay (an `ImageLabel` with a verified texture, or a radial `UIGradient`). Slow fades, rare flicker (random, not rhythmic), a tiny position jitter on damage applied to a wrapper frame.

Horror style: Keep tap targets large and text readable even though the mood is dark; the fear comes from pacing and silence, not from unreadable menus. Jump-scare overlays are full-screen frames with `Active = false` that never block input for more than a moment and have a sound cue.

Sci-fi style: Deep navy (6,14,26) panels (12,28,46), cyan accent (0,220,255), warning amber (255,170,0), alert red (255,70,70). Fonts: `Michroma`, `SciFi`, `Jura` or `TitilliumWeb` for headings; `RobotoMono` or `Code` for data readouts.

Sci-fi style: Thin 1 to 2 px strokes in the accent, chamfer-like corner brackets built from short L-shaped frames, a faint scanline `ImageLabel` or alternating-stripe overlay, a soft glow (a second larger `UIStroke` at 0.7 to 0.85 transparency), holographic panels at 0.2 to 0.4 transparency, tabular numbers, blinking caret. Open-on boot animation: lines draw in, then content fades.

Fantasy style: Parchment (222,204,164) panels on dark wood (60,40,28), gold trim (212,175,55), deep red or royal blue banners. Fonts: `Fondamento`, `Garamond`, `Antique` or `GrenzeGotisch` for titles; `Garamond` or `Merriweather` for body, dark brown text (50,35,25).

Fantasy style: Frames are a gold outer `UIStroke` over a dark inner stroke with small corners (4 to 6 px) unless a verified ornate 9-slice image is available (use `ScaleType = Slice` with `SliceCenter`). Banners and ribbons are rotated frames; rune-style icons; hover glows warm gold. Never invent decorative asset ids.

Minimal style: Near-white (250,250,250) or near-black (16,16,16) background, one accent, 1 px hairlines, no gradients, no shadows, weight and spacing instead of boxes, plenty of empty space. Fonts: `Gotham` or `Roboto` in two weights. Controls are text buttons or simple outlines; motion is a plain fade of 0.15 s.

Retro style: 8 to 16 colours, hard edges, no `UICorner`, 2 to 4 px solid borders, a solid offset drop shadow (a darker copy shifted 4 px), fonts `Arcade` or `Code`. Pixel art images use `ResampleMode = Enum.ResamplerMode.Pixelated` and integer scales. Animations step in discrete frames (use `Enum.EasingStyle.Linear` with short tweens, or step with `task.wait`).

Realistic style: Muted olive, steel or charcoal (40,44,40), amber or white HUD text (255,176,0), sharp corners, thin lines, tick marks for compass and ammo, stencil-like fonts `RobotoCondensed`, `Oswald` or `Highway`, small high-contrast text, nothing bouncy. Show only the data a real interface would: ammo, health, compass, objective.

Studded style: The Lego-brick look: a surface covered in round studs, like a baseplate or the top of a brick. Use for builder, brick, toy, obby or any 'studs' request. Build it from three things: a flat primary-colour body, a row or grid of studs on top, and a darker lower edge that gives the brick thickness.

Studded style: Palette: saturated primaries on a neutral base, for example red (196,40,28), blue (13,105,172), yellow (245,205,48), dark green (40,127,71), white and a dark grey (99,95,98). Flat fills, no gradients except a very light top-to-bottom shade of about 8 percent. Text is bold and chunky (`FredokaOne`, `LuckiestGuy` or `GothamBlack`) in white on dark bricks and near-black on yellow or white bricks.

Studded style: A stud is a circle: a `Frame` with `UICorner` at 0.5 scale, a slightly lighter fill than the body (add 18 to 25 to each channel), a 1 to 2 px darker `UIStroke` or a darker lower half to fake the rim, and an optional small lighter highlight dot at the top left. Typical size is 10 to 16 px on buttons and 24 to 32 px on large panels, with a gap of about 60 percent of the stud width.

Studded style: Few studs: for a button, a title bar or a card header, place 3 to 8 studs along the top edge with a `UIListLayout` (Horizontal, `HorizontalAlignment` Center, `Padding` about 8 px) in a transparent row that sits half over the top edge. Keep the stud row out of the click area (`Active = false`) so it never swallows taps.

Studded style: Many studs (a baseplate background, a full panel): do not create hundreds of Frames. Use one `ImageLabel` with `ScaleType = Enum.ScaleType.Tile` and a `TileSize` such as `UDim2.fromOffset(32, 32)` and a stud texture. Real-time tiling is one instance instead of hundreds. The texture must be an asset the user supplied or one you generated or confirmed with a tool; never invent an asset id. If no texture exists, build the stud once as a small `Frame`, and only repeat it with a `UIGridLayout` up to about 60 studs.

Studded style: Brick thickness: a darker copy of the body colour (about 70 percent brightness) as a base `Frame` sitting 4 to 6 px lower and behind the face, the same layered 3D-button method used in the cartoon style. On press, move the face down by that same 4 to 6 px so it sinks into the base. Corners are small (`UICorner` 4 to 8 px), because bricks are nearly square, not pill shaped.

Studded style: Layout: build panels on a grid so stud rows line up (every size a multiple of the stud pitch, for example 40 px). Align content to the stud grid, put text between stud rows rather than over studs, and keep at least 4.5:1 text contrast against the brick colour. Studs are decoration only: never let them hold text, and hide them on very small buttons where they would crowd the label.

Studded style: Variants: baseplate (green or grey, tiled studs, thin dark outline, used as a screen background or world tile), plate button (flat, one row of studs), tall brick card (studs plus a side edge shade), transparent brick (translucent tint, `BackgroundTransparency` 0.3 with a lighter outline), minifigure-yellow header with a simple face. Sounds can be a short plastic click for presses.

Skeuomorphic style: Real-material UI: wood, leather, stone, metal, paper, fabric. Use for tavern, farm, western, crafting, survival and storybook games. The material comes from a texture image or a layered fake; the structure is still a clean panel with clear hierarchy.

Skeuomorphic style: Build a panel from layers: base texture or flat fill, an inner darker border (inset) 4 to 8 px, an outer lighter border or metal trim, a soft shadow, and small fixture details such as rivets, nails or stitches (small circles or dashes placed on a grid). Materials need contrast steps: wood (120,80,45) with a lighter (170,120,70) grain highlight, leather (96,60,40) with cream (230,210,170) stitches, stone (110,110,115) with darker cracks, brushed metal (150,155,165) with a lighter top edge.

Skeuomorphic style: Textures: tile with `ScaleType.Tile` and `TileSize`, or stretch a 9-slice frame image (`ScaleType = Slice`, set `SliceCenter` in the Studio 9-slice editor) so borders keep their detail when the panel grows. Use a user-supplied or generated texture; do not invent asset ids. Without textures, fake grain with 3 to 6 thin `UIGradient` stripes or semi-transparent line Frames at 5 to 10 percent opacity.

Skeuomorphic style: Lighting: keep the highlight on the top-left and the shadow bottom-right across the whole screen. Inset elements (text fields, slots) are darker with an inner shadow; raised elements (buttons) are lighter with a drop shadow. Do not over-texture the area behind text: lay a flat darker or lighter plate under it.

Skeuomorphic style: Type: a serif or slab font for old-world looks (`Antique`, `Bodoni`, `Merriweather`-style from the Font enum), `Fantasy` for storybook headings, and a plain readable font for numbers. Keep body text 16 px or more.

Steampunk style: Brass, copper, leather, gears, gauges and rivets on dark wood or iron. Palette: brass (181,142,62), copper (184,115,51), dark iron (45,40,38), aged cream (225,210,170), a teal verdigris accent (70,140,125).

Steampunk style: Structure: a thick riveted frame (two borders, rivets at the corners and midpoints on a regular grid), a gauge-style readout for numbers (a circle `UICorner` with a needle `Frame` rotated by `Rotation`, ticks every 10 percent), and gear decorations that rotate slowly (one `ImageLabel` per gear, tween `Rotation` at 6 to 12 degrees a second, and stop the loop when the window is hidden). Keep animated gears to 2 or 3 at once.

Steampunk style: Type: `Antique`, `Fondamento`-like or slab serif for titles, a readable sans for numbers. Use engraved text: a light 1 px offset duplicate below dark text, or a `UIStroke` of 1 px in a darker tone. Buttons look like brass plates with a bevel (lighter top edge, darker bottom edge) and a level of tilt on hover of 1 to 2 degrees.

Comic style: Pop-art and comic-book UI: thick black outlines, flat bright fills, halftone dots, speech-bubble panels, burst shapes and bold slanted lettering. Use for action, superhero and party games.

Comic style: Outlines are 3 to 4 px black `UIStroke` (`LineJoinMode` Round or Miter to match the art). Fills are flat primaries with one highlight band. A hard offset shadow (a black copy 4 to 6 px down-right) replaces soft shadows. Halftone is a tiled dot image at 10 to 20 percent opacity (tile with `ScaleType.Tile`) clipped inside the panel; use a user-supplied texture, or skip it and use stripes.

Comic style: Shapes: speech bubbles with a tail (a rotated square `Frame` 45 degrees behind the bubble, same colour and stroke), burst starbursts for rewards (a rotated square duplicated at 45 degrees with the same fill), skewed title text via small `Rotation` (-3 to -6 degrees). Type: `LuckiestGuy`, `Bangers`-like or `FredokaOne`, all caps, with a thick `UIStroke` text outline. Add one onomatopoeia pop (`POW!`) on big rewards, animate it with a quick overshoot scale from 0.6 to 1.1 to 1.

Clay and candy style: Claymorphism, jelly and candy: soft puffy shapes that look moulded from clay or gummy sweets, in pastel or glossy candy colours. Use for cute, kids, bakery, pet and casual games.

Clay and candy style: Shapes: very large rounded corners (`UICorner` 0.3 to 0.5 scale), no sharp edges, slight overlap between elements. Depth comes from two inner highlights and shadows rather than one drop shadow: a lighter top-left inner `UIGradient` (lighter by 10 to 15 percent to the body colour), a darker bottom-right shade (darker by 10 to 15 percent), plus a soft outer drop shadow (a darker, lower-transparency blurred or layered copy) in the same hue, not black.

Clay and candy style: Palette: candy pinks (255,170,200), mint (170,235,210), lemon (255,235,150), sky (150,210,255), peach (255,200,170), with text in a deep tone of the same hue family (80,40,80) rather than black. Buttons squash and stretch on press (scale to 1.06 wide by 0.92 tall, then settle with a `Back` easing). Gloss highlight: a small white rounded oval at 50 to 70 percent opacity in the upper left.

Clay and candy style: Type: `FredokaOne`, `Cartoon`-style rounded fonts, 20 px and up. Keep contrast for readability: pastel on pastel fails, so put white or deep text on a mid-tone fill. Avoid heavy blur, which is costly; layered flat shapes are cheaper.

Neumorphism style: Soft UI: elements look pushed out of or into a single matte surface using a light shadow on one side and a dark shadow on the other. It looks calm but has weak contrast, so use it sparingly.

Neumorphism style: Base colour is one mid-light tone (225,230,240); raised elements share the exact same colour. Create the two shadows with two layered `Frame` copies behind the element: one lighter than the base (offset -6,-6) and one darker (offset +6,+6), or with `UIShadow` if available in the experience. Pressed state swaps to an inset look (reverse offsets, darker inner tone).

Neumorphism style: Accessibility warning: the contrast between a neumorphic control and its surface is usually under 3:1, so every control also needs a visible label, an icon, or a stronger border on the active state. Do not use it for key actions such as buy or confirm without an accent colour; give those a solid coloured fill. State (on or off, selected) must not rely on shadow alone.
Neubrutalism style: Neubrutalism: flat, loud colours, thick black borders, hard offset shadows, big type and deliberately raw layouts. Looks modern and playful; cheap to render.

Neubrutalism style: Rules: 3 to 4 px black `UIStroke` on everything, hard shadow offset (a solid black copy 6 to 8 px down-right, no blur), square or slightly rounded corners (0 to 8 px), saturated fills (yellow 255,222,89, pink 255,128,191, blue 94,160,255, mint 120,235,170) on a cream or white background, and heavy type (`GothamBlack`, `LuckiestGuy`, `Arimo` bold) in black.

Neubrutalism style: Interactions: on hover shift the face up-left 2 px and grow the shadow; on press move the face to the shadow position so the shadow disappears (mechanical click feel). Keep a strict grid with generous gaps and let one element per screen break it as an accent. Contrast is naturally high (black on bright), which makes this a good accessible style.

Y2K and retro OS style: Windows 98, Aqua gloss, early web and Y2K looks: bevelled grey windows, title bars with gradients, glossy buttons and chrome. Use for retro-computer, hacker-desktop and nostalgia games.

Y2K and retro OS style: Win98: grey (192,192,192) window face, 2 px bevel (white top-left, dark grey (128,128,128) and black bottom-right lines made with four thin `Frame` strips or two nested frames), a navy-to-blue title bar (`UIGradient` from (0,0,128) to (16,132,208)) with white bold text and three small square control buttons, `Code` or `Arcade` fonts at crisp sizes. Pressed buttons invert the bevel. No `UICorner` and no soft shadows.

Y2K and retro OS style: Aqua and Y2K gloss: a pill button with a vertical `UIGradient` (lighter top, deeper bottom), a white semi-transparent oval highlight on the upper half (clipped inside, 40 to 60 percent opacity), a 1 px darker stroke, and a faint reflection below. Chrome is a grey-white vertical gradient with a dark horizontal band at 50 percent. Keep it to a few big shapes; many glossy overlays cost transparency overdraw.
Pixel style: Pixel-art UI done properly. Choose a base pixel size (for example 2 or 3 screen pixels per art pixel) and make every size, position and font a whole multiple of it, so edges never blur.

Pixel style: Images: set `ResampleMode = Enum.ResamplerMode.Pixelated` on every pixel `ImageLabel` and `ImageButton`, and scale them by whole numbers only (2x, 3x, 4x). Borders and bevels are 1 art pixel wide, drawn as Frames of that size or as a 9-slice (`ScaleType.Slice`) of a small pixel frame image. Avoid `UICorner`; make stepped corners by cutting the 4 corner pixels with small Frames matching the background, or bake them into the image.

Pixel style: Palette: a small fixed palette (limit to 8 to 16 colours), dither with a checkerboard pixel image rather than gradients. Fonts: `Arcade`, `Code` or a pixel font uploaded by the user, at sizes where one font pixel equals one art pixel. Animation: step frames with a sprite sheet (`ImageRectOffset` and `ImageRectSize` change on a timer, 6 to 12 frames per second) and snap movement to the pixel grid. Icons are 16x16 or 32x32 art scaled up.

Paper and sticker style: Hand-made looks: notebook paper, scrapbook, stickers, torn tape, hand-drawn doodle borders, parchment and manuscript pages. Use for storybook, diary, quest-journal and cozy games.

Paper and sticker style: Paper: warm off-white (245,238,220) or parchment (228,206,160) base with a slightly darker edge (a `UIStroke` of 1 to 2 px, or an inner gradient from the edges at 10 to 15 percent), a soft drop shadow, and a few degrees of rotation (-2 to 2) per card so they look placed by hand. Lines: thin horizontal rules every 28 to 32 px (tiled image or Frames), a red margin line for notebooks.

Paper and sticker style: Stickers: a white or cream outline around a colourful icon (a larger copy of the icon in white behind it, or a thick light `UIStroke`), a gentle drop shadow, and a small peel highlight on one corner. Tape: a semi-transparent rectangle (`BackgroundTransparency` 0.35, pale yellow) rotated 8 to 15 degrees over a card's top edge. Type: handwriting-style fonts (`Kalam`-like, `Fondamento`, `Sarpanch` are examples from the Font enum; check the enum) for titles, readable sans for details. For manuscript or parchment, drop caps (a larger first letter via rich text `<font size="36">`) and ornamental dividers.

Blueprint and terminal style: Technical looks: blueprint sheets, command-line terminals, hacker consoles and engineering readouts. Blueprint: deep blue (20,50,110) with thin white or pale cyan lines, a faint grid (lines every 24 to 32 px at 15 to 20 percent opacity), dimension arrows and labelled callouts. Terminal: near-black (12,14,12), phosphor green (60,255,120) or amber (255,176,0) text, `Code` font, a blinking block cursor.

Blueprint and terminal style: Terminal text: use a monospace `Code` font, left aligned, line height of 1.1 to 1.2, and output that prints in lines (add one line at a time every 0.03 to 0.08 s). For a typed effect, set the text then tween `MaxVisibleGraphemes` from 0 to the full length; with rich text on, this does not print tags. Blinking cursor: toggle a Frame's `BackgroundTransparency` every 0.5 s, and stop when hidden. A scanline overlay is a tiled image at 5 to 8 percent opacity.

Blueprint and terminal style: Blueprint details: all lines 1 px, no fills except pale tints, text in uppercase small caps (the `<sc>` rich text tag), corner crop marks, and a title block in the bottom-right with project, scale and date fields. Keep contrast high: pale cyan (180,230,255) text on the blue passes comfortably.
Holographic and iridescent style: Foil, hologram, chrome and iridescent looks for rare rewards and futuristic panels. The colour shifts with angle, which you fake with moving gradients.

Holographic and iridescent style: Iridescent fill: a `UIGradient` with 4 to 6 `ColorSequence` keypoints cycling through pink (255,150,220), cyan (150,230,255), lemon (255,240,160), lavender (190,170,255) and back; animate it by tweening `UIGradient.Offset` from (-1,0) to (1,0) over 2 to 4 s, repeating. Foil sheen: a diagonal bright band (a narrow white `UIGradient` strip with transparency, rotated 20 to 30 degrees) sweeping across once every few seconds, not constantly.

Holographic and iridescent style: Keep text on a solid or darker plate so the shifting colours do not wreck readability. Hologram panels (sci-fi): translucent cyan fill (`BackgroundTransparency` 0.6 to 0.8), a bright 1 px edge, faint scanlines and small flicker (transparency jumps of 0.05 to 0.1, not full blinking). Limit animated gradients to a few visible elements; each running tween costs time.
Aurora and gradient style: Soft multi-colour gradient backgrounds: aurora, mesh-style glows and sunset washes behind clean UI. Use as screen backdrops for menus, loading screens and profile pages.

Aurora and gradient style: Mesh-like glow: stack 3 to 5 large circular blobs (`Frame` with `UICorner` 0.5, size 40 to 70 percent of the screen) in different hues, each with a radial-looking `UIGradient` that fades to full transparency at the edges, over a dark base (15,15,30). Overlap them and move them slowly (position drifts of 3 to 6 percent over 10 to 20 s, `Sine` easing). Avoid hard edges and avoid stacking many full-screen transparent layers; flatten the final backdrop to one image if possible for mobile.

Aurora and gradient style: On top, keep panels clean and legible: a dark translucent plate (`BackgroundTransparency` 0.3 to 0.5) or a solid card, white text, and one accent colour pulled from the backdrop. `UIGradient.Rotation` and per-keypoint `ColorSequence` keep gradients cheap compared with images. Check text contrast at the brightest part of the gradient.
Low-poly and geometric style: Angular, faceted, flat-shaded shapes with a limited palette. Use for abstract, space, nature and indie looks.

Low-poly and geometric style: Faceted shapes: triangles and cut corners from rotated squares, `UIGradient` rotated to a hard two-stop split to fake a lit and shaded facet, or imported triangle images. Panels use chamfered corners (rotate a small square 45 degrees at each corner in the background colour) rather than `UICorner`. Palette: 4 to 6 related hues with two shades each, flat fills and no outlines.

Low-poly and geometric style: Typography is geometric sans, medium weight, generous spacing. Keep alignment strict and symmetrical, use diagonal dividers sparingly (a rotated `Frame` clipped by its parent), and animate with linear or `Quad` moves in short, crisp steps.

Dark mode and bento layouts: Dark UI: never pure black on pure white text. Use a surface ladder (page 15,17,22; card 24,27,34; raised 34,38,47; highest 46,51,62), body text at about 87 percent white (222,224,230), secondary text at about 60 percent, and one desaturated accent. Elevation is shown by lighter surfaces, not bigger shadows. Test contrast, since 4.5:1 for body text still applies.

Dark mode and bento layouts: Bento layouts: a grid of rounded tiles of different sizes (1x1, 2x1, 2x2) that tile a screen like a lunch box, each tile one idea (stat, shop item, daily reward, news). Build with a parent Frame, a fixed gap (12 to 16 px) and tile sizes as exact multiples of a column unit; use `UIGridLayout` for equal tiles, or place unequal tiles by scale. Tiles share one corner radius and one padding value, and reflow to a single column on narrow phone screens.
Anime and gacha style: Anime, RNG and gacha games: character art, rarity glow, shiny backgrounds, ornate frames and speed lines. Rarity must be obvious at a glance.

Anime and gacha style: Card: a tall frame with a rarity-coloured border (2 to 4 px `UIStroke`), a top-to-bottom `UIGradient` tint, a character image masked inside rounded corners (use `ClipsDescendants` on a square frame, or a `CanvasGroup` if you need rounded clipping), a name plate at the bottom, and rarity stars or a gem. Reveal sequence: dim the screen, show a pulsing shape, burst, then the card flips (scale X from 1 to 0 and back to 1 with the face swapped at 0).

Anime and gacha style: Rarity colours, a common convention: common grey (170,170,170), uncommon green (90,200,90), rare blue (70,140,255), epic purple (170,90,255), legendary orange or gold (255,170,40), mythic red or pink (255,70,110). Do not rely on colour alone: add a label, star count or border pattern too. Speed lines are thin rotated Frames behind the art. Keep reveal animations skippable after the first second.

StyleSheet: Roblox has a CSS-like styling system: `StyleSheet` and `StyleRule` instances, a `StyleLink` that applies a sheet to a `ScreenGui` or other GUI root, and `StyleDerive` to inherit from another sheet. Selectors work on class names, tags and names; rules can use design tokens so a whole game re-themes by changing one value. Before writing it, open the StyleSheet, StyleRule and StyleLink class pages (and the 'Styling' guide) in the docs and use the exact syntax shown there; it has changed between releases.

StyleSheet: Use it for large UI sets that share a look (many screens, themes, dark and light). For one or two screens, a small Lua module with a palette table and constructor functions (`Theme.new`, `makeButton(props)`) is simpler and is fine. Do not mix both for the same properties on the same objects: a rule and a script fighting over `BackgroundColor3` is a bug.

StyleSheet: Style transitions let state changes (hover, pressed) animate without scripts. Keep colours, radii, fonts and paddings as tokens, keep structure in the instances, and keep per-element exceptions to a minimum.

3D in UI: Goal: UI that shows real 3D objects (item icons, pets, characters, weapons, currency piles, shop previews) the way big simulator shops do. The AI makes the 3D object itself from Parts (or a toolbox model), then shows it inside the UI with a `ViewportFrame`. Do this whenever the user says 3D icon, model in the UI, item preview, pet or character card, voxel or blocky art, or shows a shop with 3D renders.

3D in UI: Which method: (1) static icon that never moves, and many of them: build the model once, show it in a `ViewportFrame`, and keep at most one visible per row or page; if the same icon appears dozens of times, a pre-rendered image is cheaper. (2) Inspect, rotate, hover or equip preview: `ViewportFrame` with a live model. (3) World-space screens (a model that is part of the map): `SurfaceGui` or `BillboardGui` instead. Developers report that a `ViewportFrame` costs more than an `ImageLabel` because it renders to its own target, and that dozens at once hurt weak devices (a community report, not an official limit), so page the list and create viewports only for the visible page.

3D in UI: Setup, in this order: create the `ViewportFrame` (transparent background if it sits on a gradient card: `BackgroundTransparency = 1`), create a `Camera`, parent it to the viewport, and assign it to `ViewportFrame.CurrentCamera` (the property is not replicated, so do this on the client). Clone the model, parent the clone into the viewport (objects must be parented to the viewport to render), and place it at a known point such as the origin. Without the `CurrentCamera` assignment the model shows tiny or not at all. Do not parent the live workspace object itself; always clone.

3D in UI: Clean the clone before showing it: remove every `Script`, `LocalScript`, `ModuleScript`, `Sound`, `ParticleEmitter` and `Light` inside it, set parts to `Anchored = true`, `CanCollide = false`, `CanQuery = false`, `CastShadow = false`, and drop tiny parts nobody can see at icon size. A 64 px icon gains nothing from small details, so a model of 5 to 40 parts reads as well as one of 400.

3D in UI: Fit the model to the frame with maths, never by hand-picked numbers. Use `model:GetBoundingBox()` (returns a CFrame and a size) or `GetExtentsSize()`. With the camera's vertical field of view `vFov = math.rad(camera.FieldOfView)` and the frame's aspect ratio `a = AbsoluteSize.X / AbsoluteSize.Y`: `hFov = 2 * math.atan(a * math.tan(vFov / 2))`, `distH = (size.Y / 2) / math.tan(vFov / 2)`, `distW = (size.X / 2) / math.tan(hFov / 2)`, distance = `math.max(distH, distW)` plus the model depth `size.Z / 2` and about 10 percent padding. Place the camera at `center + lookDirection * distance` with `CFrame.lookAt(camPos, center)`. A bounding-sphere fit never crops but leaves more empty space; a camera-aligned box is tighter if the model is rotated. Re-measure after `ScaleTo`, and recompute only when the model or frame size changes (not every frame), except while orbiting.

3D in UI: Framing for cards: a three-quarter view looks best for creatures and props: camera about 20 to 30 degrees above and 25 to 40 degrees to the side of the front. Characters stand centred with the feet near the bottom and about 10 to 15 percent breathing room. A slightly low field of view (30 to 40) flattens perspective and looks more like a render; the default 70 distorts close up. Keep the origin the same for every item so cards line up.

3D in UI: Lighting is fixed and limited: viewports use their own light settings (`Ambient` default (200,200,200), `LightColor` default (140,140,140), `LightDirection` default (-1,-1,-1)); there are no shadows and no post-effects, and Neon and Glass materials render at the lowest quality. So avoid relying on Neon or Glass inside viewports. To make a model pop: raise `LightColor` toward (200,200,200) and lower `Ambient` to (150,150,160) for contrast, point `LightDirection` from the upper left, and use `ImageColor3` to tint the whole render (for example a grey tint for locked items). Flat-coloured `Plastic` or `SmoothPlastic` parts with good colour contrast look best.

3D in UI: Spin and hover: rotate the model (for example `PivotTo(model:GetPivot() * CFrame.Angles(0, dt * 1.5, 0))`) or orbit the camera, from one shared `RunService.RenderStepped` connection that updates only visible viewports; never block a loop per item (a `while` loop around a `RenderStepped:Wait()` stops the rest from running). Spin only the hovered, selected or equipped item, 20 to 40 degrees a second, and stop and disconnect when the window closes. Hover zoom: tween the camera distance by 5 to 8 percent over 0.1 s.

3D in UI: Known quirks (community reports): a viewport can freeze and stop redrawing until the viewport or its camera changes, and nudging the camera's `FieldOfView` by a tiny amount forces a redraw; if moving the camera's `CFrame` does nothing, assign a camera again to `CurrentCamera`. The viewport size is reported capped at about 1024 by 1024, so very large frames stretch. Edges can show an anti-alias fringe, so avoid pure-white models on pure-white cards.

3D in UI: Characters and rigs: accessories and welds need physics to settle, so parent the rig inside a `WorldModel` (it extends limited physics to children) for at least one `Heartbeat` before showing it, and when cloning an avatar clone its descendants, not only its direct children. Animations inside viewports are unreliable (reports of animations playing but not rendering); prefer a static pose, a `PivotTo` rotation or a bob built from tweens. For avatar previews use `HumanoidDescription` applied to a rig that is already inside the `WorldModel`.

3D in UI: Sources of models: (a) build from Parts, which is the default and most reliable; (b) the Creator Store (Toolbox) if the Studio asset tools are connected: search for the object, prefer verified creators and low part counts, insert it, then strip scripts and sounds before use because models can carry scripts; (c) `InsertService:LoadAsset` or `AssetService:LoadAssetAsync` at runtime for an asset id the user owns or has confirmed; (d) generated meshes if a generate tool is available. Never invent asset ids and never claim a toolbox asset exists without the search result.

3D in UI: Build the model like an artist: a silhouette first (3 to 7 big shapes), then 2 to 3 secondary details, then eyes, face or accent colour. Use a limited palette of 3 to 5 colours with one shade lighter and darker for faces and a bright accent. Everything on a shared grid (multiples of 0.5 or 1 stud) so it reads as bricks or voxels. Group the parts in a `Model`, set `PrimaryPart` and `WorldPivot` so it rotates around its centre, name the model, and keep one model per item in `ReplicatedStorage` (a folder such as `UIModels`) to clone from.

3D in UI: Blocky voxel creature recipe: body (box), head (box about 0.8 times the body width), two eyes (small dark boxes plus 1 white box each), 2 or 4 legs (boxes), optional tail, ears, horns, hat or accessory, a colour per body region. Slightly oversized head and eyes read as cute at small sizes. Mixed parts of 0.2 to 0.4 stud steps make a studded look. Add `SurfaceAppearance`-free flat materials so lighting stays predictable.

3D in UI: Works in every style and every kind of screen, not only shops or studded looks: 3D can be the hero of any UI. Use it for a main-menu character or logo, a pet or avatar card, a loot or gacha reveal, a weapon or tool inspector, a vehicle or map-piece selector, a level or world picker, a quest-giver portrait in dialogue, a rotating currency icon on a HUD, a hologram in a sci-fi panel, a trophy in a leaderboard, or a game-over scene. Decide first whether 3D adds value; flat art is better for tiny repeated icons.

3D in UI: Match the 3D to the chosen style, and keep the frame, text and colours from that style section. Cartoon or studded: blocky chunky models, flat bright colours. Sleek modern or minimal: single-colour smooth models on a plain plate, slow rotation, no clutter. Horror: dark desaturated models, low `Ambient`, red-tinted `ImageColor3`, a faint vignette overlay. Sci-fi and holographic: a cyan `ImageColor3` tint, thin outline frames, scanlines on top. Fantasy and skeuomorphic: warm lighting, ornate frame around the viewport. Pixel: very low-part, blocky models with flat colours and a limited palette, so they sit well beside pixel art. Glass: model over a translucent plate. The 3D never replaces the UI structure; it sits inside normal frames, cards and buttons.

3D in UI: Layer it like any other element: a card background, then the transparent `ViewportFrame`, then text and buttons above it with higher `ZIndex`. Keep click handling on a transparent button over the viewport (the viewport is not the button). Build 3D only when the UI that holds it is open, and destroy the clone and viewport when it closes.

Studded shop screen: Reference look: the studded blocky simulator shop (a blue studded title bar with a red close square, stacked gradient offer rows, white bold text with a thick black outline, lime price buttons with a stud texture, 3D blocky item renders on small gradient tiles, on a studded floor). Build any shop, pack, upgrade or reward screen in this look with these steps.

Studded shop screen: Window: about 580 by 380 px on desktop, centred, with a 3 px near-black `UIStroke` and a lighter grey-blue frame (a mid-grey (150,160,175) panel with a dark border) around a scrolling list. Title bar: a blue (30,140,255) bar about 48 px high with a tiled stud texture on the whole bar (one `ImageLabel` with `ScaleType.Tile`, `TileSize` about 18 by 18, studs a few percent lighter than the bar), a small icon (basket, gem, star) and the title in white bold with a black stroke, left aligned; the close button is a red (230,40,30) square about 40 px with a white X, a black stroke, and a darker bottom edge. Corner radius is tiny (0 to 6 px); the look is square and chunky.

Studded shop screen: Offer rows: each row is a full-width card about 110 to 130 px high with its own left-to-right `UIGradient` (green (40,220,120) to cyan (30,200,240); blue to cyan; red (230,50,60) to purple (170,50,230); yellow to orange) and a 3 px black stroke. Layout inside: the visual on the left (a lone 3D icon, or a row of 3 square item tiles), the title and tags top right, the price button bottom right. Use a `UIListLayout` with 6 to 8 px gaps in an `AutomaticCanvasSize = Y` `ScrollingFrame`.

Studded shop screen: Item tiles: three squares about 100 px each, each with its own gradient (cyan to blue; yellow to orange; lime to yellow) and a 2 px black stroke, the 3D render filling about 85 percent of the tile (a `ViewportFrame` over the gradient, transparent background), the name in small white bold text with a black stroke at the bottom, and a bonus line such as `+$100K` in white. Items differ by hue so a row reads as three separate things.

Studded shop screen: Price button: a lime (170,240,40) to green (80,200,50) vertical `UIGradient`, a 3 px black stroke, a studded texture overlay at 10 to 15 percent opacity, a darker (60,150,40) bottom edge 4 px thick for depth, and the currency icon next to the number in white bold with a black stroke (about 24 to 28 px). Pressing moves the face down 3 to 4 px. Discount or limited-time tags are small lime-yellow (200,255,40) text with a black stroke above the price.

Studded shop screen: Text: heavy rounded font (`FredokaOne`, `LuckiestGuy` or `GothamBlack`), white with a 2 to 3 px black `UIStroke` (`ApplyStrokeMode` Contextual), sizes 14 px for tags, 20 to 24 px for names, 32 to 40 px for big values like `Luck = 1x`. Secondary tags (limited time, descriptions) use lime-yellow (255,230,0) and may wrap in 2 to 3 lines; keep every line readable against its gradient (check the darkest and lightest end of the gradient).

Studded shop screen: Scene: the studded floor is a `Part` with a studs texture or the `Studs` surface; the background sky is the game's own. The HUD cash readout sits bottom-left in a dark translucent plate with the money icon and green text. Close with the red X, and open and close with the usual scale pop (0.92 to 1, 0.2 s). All sizes are scale-based with `UIAspectRatioConstraint` and `UISizeConstraint` so the window fits phones.

Studded shop screen: Make it with real 3D: for each item, build or fetch a blocky model (see 3D in UI), show it in a transparent `ViewportFrame` over the tile gradient, rotate it slowly only while hovered, and use the same camera angle for every item. If the user supplies an image of a shop, copy its structure and colours, not its art or branding.

Complete screens and shops: A screen is not finished until it is full and every control is wired. Never ship an empty content area, a Buy button with nothing selected, tabs with nothing behind them, or a panel waiting for data that never comes. Fill every list and grid with real entries from the game's own data; if the game has no data yet, create one clearly named config table (for example `ShopItems` with id, name, description, price, currency, icon, rarity, tab) with at least 6 believable entries per tab, build the UI from it, and tell the user where to edit it.

Complete screens and shops: Test with stress data before finishing: zero items, one item, many items (30+), very long names, a missing picture, a price the player cannot afford, an owned item, a locked item. Each must look intentional. Real empty states (nothing owned yet) need a headline, one short friendly line, a small picture and one action that fills the screen; never a blank panel. Loading: use a skeleton of the real layout when you know its shape, a spinner when you do not; never leave a blank panel.

Complete screens and shops: Shop anatomy: a header with the title and a close button; the currency the player has, always visible; tabs for categories; a scrolling grid or list of item cards; and a detail or purchase area. Put the best offer first and make it larger or set apart (a hero card); group related items by size and spacing; make premium or limited items visibly different (gold stripe, badge); show at most about 6 to 8 offers before scrolling or paging; the price must be visible without scrolling.

Complete screens and shops: Item card: a clear picture of the item, a name that says what it is or does ('Sugar Rush Boost', not 'Item 3'), one short line of what it does (function, not backstory), the price with its currency icon, and a state: for sale, owned, equipped, locked ('unlocks at level 5' shown directly, not hidden behind a tap), or unaffordable (price in red, button greyed with the reason). Badges such as New or Best Deal must contrast with the card.

Complete screens and shops: Buy button: bound to the selected item and says what it will do ('Buy Lollipop Pack - 120'). With nothing selected it is disabled and says 'Pick an item' (or the first item is selected by default). When the player cannot afford it, it shows how many more are needed. Pressing it disables the button while the server checks; then show what was gained and how to use it (toast or flash on the card). Ask for confirmation only for expensive or irreversible buys. The server validates the purchase.

Complete screens and shops: Tabs: 2 to 6 tabs (4 to 5 on phones); names say what is inside and fit the shop (a candy shop uses Candy, Boosts, Cosmetics, not unrelated words like Coins unless coins are sold); every tab has content; the selected tab is shown with at least two cues (a filled colour, heavier or larger text, an underline or raised shape) never colour alone; inactive tabs stay readable (text contrast 4.5:1 against the tab, or 3:1 if the text is large and bold); each tab is at least 44 to 48 px high and 80 to 96 px wide with the label not truncated (leave about 20 percent spare width); switching tabs keeps the scroll area and takes under 0.3 s.

Complete screens and shops: Reach and layout: the shop opens in 3 taps or fewer from the HUD; the shop button is labelled with text, not only an icon; the window is a modal with a dimmed backdrop and a square close button (red with a white X is the familiar convention) at the top right of the panel, not hidden by other elements. Related buttons share size and spacing; the main action is the biggest or brightest thing in its area.

Contrast check: Measure, do not eyeball. For each text and background pair (and for icons, borders and tab labels) compute the WCAG contrast ratio. Linearise each channel c (0 to 1): `c <= 0.03928 and c/12.92 or ((c+0.055)/1.055)^2.4`; luminance `L = 0.2126*R + 0.7152*G + 0.0722*B`; ratio `= (Lbright + 0.05) / (Ldark + 0.05)`. Write a small helper in Luau, run it over every pair in the screen, and fix failures.

Contrast check: Targets: body text 4.5:1; large text (about 24 px regular or 18.7 px bold and up) 3:1; icons, borders, input outlines, focus rings and the selected-versus-unselected difference 3:1; do not round up (4.47 fails). Inactive or disabled controls are exempt by the standard but must still be readable enough to know what they are, and they must say why they are inactive. Logos and decorative text are exempt.

Contrast check: Gradients and images: test the worst place under the text, which is the lightest and darkest end of a gradient or the busiest part of a picture. A `UIStroke` outline or a plate under the text can rescue a pair, and the outline must itself contrast with the text (white text with a dark outline, or dark text with a light outline). Same-hue pairs fail most often: pink text on a pink tab, green text on a green card, dark green art on a bright green card. Use a deep tone of the hue for text on light plates, or white on a deep tone.

Contrast check: Softening: pure black text (0,0,0) can be replaced by a deep tint of the UI hue (for example deep raspberry on pink, navy on blue) which looks richer and still passes. Pure white on very bright colours (yellow, lime, cyan) usually fails, so use a dark text or a dark outline there. Saturated neon-like colours next to each other vibrate and look muddy at distance; reduce the number of saturated colours and use one baseline colour with one contrasting accent.

Contrast check: Minimum sizes: text no smaller than 12 px on any device, 14 px or more for body text on phones; `UITextSizeConstraint.MinTextSize` should never be below 9 (the docs warn text is hard to read), and in practice not below 12. Do not rely on colour alone for state; add an icon, shape or label.

Text fitting: Text must never overflow or clip. Tiles and buttons need a stated text policy: one line with `TextTruncate = AtEnd` for names; wrapped two lines with `TextWrapped = true` and a fixed height for descriptions; or a fixed text size with the label sized to fit.

Text fitting: `TextScaled = true` ties the text size to the label's height, makes sizes vary between labels with different string lengths, and shrinks long strings until `TextFits` becomes false; it also turns on `TextWrapped` implicitly. Use it only with a `UITextSizeConstraint` (min 12, a sensible max) and check the result. More predictable: fixed `TextSize` per role (title, name, price, caption) with a `UIScale` for device scaling, then check `TextBounds` against `AbsoluteSize` and reduce the size step by step until it fits (stop at the minimum and truncate instead). Re-check on `GetPropertyChangedSignal('AbsoluteSize')`.

Text fitting: A name cut off at a tile edge ('onelo Cactus') is a failure. Give names room (width of the tile minus padding), allow two lines when the card is tall enough, or truncate with an ellipsis; never let text sit under the edge of its container. Keep text and picture separate children so a long name cannot push the art. Parent text in a frame with `ClipsDescendants` only as a last resort, because clipped text still looks wrong.

Text fitting: Fonts: one display font for titles and buttons, one readable font for body text and numbers; a decorative or stylised font only for titles and big headers (stylised fonts hurt reading in instructions). Avoid very wide faces for body text. Bold weights for small button text. Numbers that change (prices, counts) use a font with even digit widths and a fixed label width so layouts do not jump. Left-align reading text, centre only short labels.

Text fitting: Outlines: light text on a coloured plate gets a 2 to 3 px dark `UIStroke` (use `ApplyStrokeMode = Contextual`); a thick cream or white outline suits candy and cartoon titles because it separates the letters from busy art. Do not outline everything; small body text with a thick outline turns to mush.

Candy and sweets style: For candy, sweets, bakery, ice cream, dessert, chocolate and sugar themed games. The look is glossy, swollen and edible: rounded shapes, saturated fills with a bright highlight, a thick light outline, and a sweet palette with several accent colours, not one pink. Everything pink on pink is the main failure to avoid.
