code-quality.name: Code Quality — mandatory Roblox scripting standard
code-quality.description: Always use when writing, fixing or reviewing Roblox scripts: engineering practice, architecture and lifecycle, patterns, typed classes, error handling, player and event lifecycle, testing, style and review, plus security, data, purchases and performance.
code-quality.whenToUse: Always use for any Roblox code: writing, fixing, refactoring or reviewing scripts, modules, remotes, data saving, purchases, player and character handling, structure and performance.
steps: Mandatory standard for every Roblox script. Built from the official Roblox docs (security, remotes, type checking, native code generation, Parallel Luau, performance, player data and purchases) and community practice.
Architecture: The server owns game state, rules, progression, currency and rewards. The client renders and sends intent only.
Architecture: Server-only code and data go in ServerScriptService or ServerStorage, never ReplicatedStorage (every client downloads it and can decompile it).
Architecture: One script per job. Logic lives in ModuleScripts that return a table; scripts only wire modules together and connect events.
Architecture: Require modules in a serial context, never during a parallel phase. Avoid circular requires.
Architecture: Expose the minimum: keep helpers local, return only the public API.
Architecture: Read the existing scripts, naming and folder layout first and match them. Do not duplicate a system that already exists.
Types: Start every new script with --!strict. Use --!nonstrict only for old code that cannot be typed yet.
Types: Annotate all function parameters and returns and any shared table shape. Share types with export type in the module.
Types: Use ? for optional values and refine with an explicit nil or typeof check. Use :: casts only when verified; never cast to any to silence a warning.
Types: There is no table type: write {T} for lists, {[K]: V} for maps, {Field: T} for records. Never mix numeric and string keys in one table.
Types: Fix every Script Analysis warning you introduce.
Security: An exploiter can fire any remote at any rate with any arguments, fire Touched and ProximityPrompt at any range, own their character and unanchored parts, and read any replicated script.

Security: Every server remote handler, in order: check argument count and types with typeof, reject NaN and infinity, clamp or reject out-of-range numbers, validate enums and string length against an allow-list, confirm the player is allowed (alive, owns the item, has the level), confirm the action is possible (cooldown, range, state), then act.
Security: The client never sends prices, damage, rewards, results or other players' data. The server looks up the real values.
Security: Rate limit every remote per player (minimum interval or token bucket) and drop or kick on abuse. Keep a server cooldown even if the client has one.
Security: Validate distance and line of sight on the server before pickups, hits and interactions. Never trust a client-reported Touched on its own.
Security: WalkSpeed, JumpPower and similar humanoid properties are client-replicated and can be changed by the client. Never use them as security; sanity check position and speed on the server.

Security: Prefer RemoteEvent for one-way calls. Avoid server-to-client RemoteFunction calls (a client can error, disconnect or never return and stall the server thread); if unavoidable use pcall with a timeout path. Only one OnServerInvoke runs per RemoteFunction.

Security: Remote payloads: tables are copied, metatables stripped, functions arrive as nil, non-string keys become strings, nil inside tables breaks arrays, instances the receiver cannot see arrive as nil. Send plain arrays or plain dictionaries of simple values. Do not mix numeric and string keys.
Security: UnreliableRemoteEvent only for continuous, disposable data under about 1000 bytes, with a sequence number so old messages are ignored. Never for purchases, damage or required state changes.
Security: Hiding a UI or checking inside a LocalScript is not security. Never put secrets, keys or webhook URLs in client-visible code.

Data and purchases: Use a session-locked, proven approach (an established module such as ProfileStore or ProfileService, or your own over UpdateAsync). Do reads and writes through UpdateAsync where a lock or merge is needed.

Data and purchases: Wrap every DataStore call in pcall with retries: exponential backoff plus jitter, a capped delay and a capped attempt count. Process requests per key in order so a retry cannot overwrite newer data.
Data and purchases: Never save data that failed to load or is still loading. On a failed load use default data marked as errored and never save it over the real record.

Data and purchases: Save on PlayerRemoving, on a periodic loop with a random first-save offset per player, and in game:BindToClose (save all players in parallel, return only when all finish, stay inside the 30 second limit). Clear a player's data from memory after the final save.

Data and purchases: ProcessReceipt: wait for the player's data to load (stop if they leave), check the PurchaseId against recorded ones, grant in memory, record the id, save, and return PurchaseGranted only if the save succeeded, otherwise NotProcessedYet. Never grant twice for one id.
Data and purchases: Keep a schema version in saved data and migrate on load. Give new fields defaults with a reconcile step.
Performance: Prefer events over polling. No while true do task.wait() loops that check state; connect to the signal.
Performance: Per-frame work stays tiny (about 16 ms per frame at 60 FPS). Heartbeat for simulation; RenderStepped only for camera and visuals that must beat the render.
Performance: Cache repeated lookups (services, FindFirstChild, GetChildren) in locals outside hot paths. Use CollectionService tags instead of scanning Workspace.
Performance: Split long work across frames. Use table.create, table.insert, table.concat and string.format instead of building strings in loops.
Performance: Create instances unparented, set properties, then set Parent last. Pool frequently spawned objects. Clean temporary ones with Debris or task.delay.
Performance: Use --!native or @native only on hot numeric functions (maths, Vector3, buffers) with typed arguments, after measuring with the Script Profiler. Never whole large scripts.

Performance: Use Parallel Luau only for heavy independent work (NPC logic, raycast checks, generation): scripts under Actors, compute in the parallel phase, change instances in the serial phase, ConnectParallel, no require and no DataModel writes in parallel.
Performance: Do not put heavy content in ReplicatedStorage. Write code that copes with StreamingEnabled (WaitForChild with a timeout, PersistentLoaded, model streaming mode).
Memory and cleanup: Every Connect has an owner that disconnects it (a Maid, Janitor or Trove, or the project's helper), tied to Destroying, the player leaving or the character being removed.
Memory and cleanup: Clear per-player tables on PlayerRemoving and per-character state on removal or death. Destroy instances you create when finished. Cap every table or queue that can grow.
Modern API only: task.spawn, task.defer, task.delay, task.wait. Never wait, spawn or delay.

Modern API only: workspace:Raycast with RaycastParams, not FindPartOnRay. Animator:LoadAnimation, not Humanoid:LoadAnimation. Constraints (LinearVelocity, AlignPosition and so on), not BodyVelocity or BodyForce. TweenService, ContextActionService, UserInputService. PlayerAdded plus a loop over existing players so nobody is missed.
Modern API only: For OverlapParams use ExcludeInstances or IncludeInstances; FilterDescendantsInstances and FilterType are superseded.
Modern API only: Instance.new then set properties; do not pass a parent argument.
Modern API only: os.clock for timing, workspace:GetServerTimeNow for synchronised time. Do not trust os.time on the client for gameplay.
Modern API only: If unsure an API exists or its signature is right, look it up in the Roblox documentation first. Do not invent members. Mark anything unconfirmed.

Errors and style: Fail fast on programmer errors with assert or error and a clear message. Wrap I/O and external calls in pcall and handle the failure path explicitly. Never swallow an error silently. Use warn for recoverable problems; remove debug prints before finishing.

Errors and style: PascalCase for services, types, classes and public members; camelCase for locals, functions and private values; UPPER_SNAKE for constants. Early returns instead of deep nesting, small single-purpose functions, no magic numbers. Comments explain why. Match the project's StyLua and Selene settings if present.

Data limits (official): store name, key and scope are at most 50 characters; a serialised value is at most 4,194,304 characters (measure with HttpService:JSONEncode and do not pre-compress); per key, reads are 25 MB per minute and writes 4 MB per minute; the per-server budget is 60 + 40 x players requests per minute for reads and for writes (list 5 + 2 x players); each request queue holds 30 and overflow is dropped (errors 301 to 306), so back off and retry later.

Data errors (official): a failed write may still have happened, so verify with a fresh read before retrying a non-idempotent write. 403 means Studio API access is off; 401 and 402 mean the server is shutting down so do not retry; 105 means the value is too large; throttled and internal-server errors retry with exponential backoff. Spread writes across keys, because many requests to one key or store can be throttled. Studio run mode has lower limits, so test in a published place.

Scheduling (official): task.spawn runs the function immediately; task.defer runs it at the end of the current resume point in the same frame; task.delay runs on the first Heartbeat after at least the duration (a minimum, not exact); task.wait resumes on the next Heartbeat and returns the real elapsed time; task.cancel stops a thread that has not run yet. task.synchronize and task.desynchronize only work in scripts under an Actor.

Raycasting (official): workspace:Raycast(origin, direction, params): the direction's length sets the distance (maximum 15000 studs); between two points use target minus origin. A miss returns nil, so always check the result. RaycastParams uses FilterDescendantsInstances with FilterType Exclude or Include, plus IgnoreWater and CollisionGroup. Parts with CanQuery false are ignored. With streaming, distant unstreamed parts can be missed on the client and imposter models cannot be hit.

CollectionService (official): connect GetInstanceAddedSignal(tag), then loop GetTagged(tag) for instances that already exist, keep one connection per instance, and clean up in GetInstanceRemovedSignal. GetTagged skips instances with no parent and has no guaranteed order. All tags on an instance replicate together, so a server tag change overwrites client-added tags. Use HasTag for a single tag, not GetTags.

Streaming (official): streaming applies only to Workspace descendants, never ReplicatedStorage. Model streaming modes are Nonatomic (default), Atomic (the whole model arrives together, so WaitForChild on the model and not its parts), Persistent (rare; wait for Workspace.PersistentLoaded) and PersistentPerPlayer. Streaming out sets Parent to nil and loses local-only changes; client-created instances are not streamed out. Never set StreamingMinRadius equal to StreamingTargetRadius. StreamingIntegrityMode PauseOutsideLoadedArea is recommended.

ProximityPrompt (official): Triggered(player) fires on the server, but an exploiter can trigger it at any range, so re-check distance, cooldown and state in the handler. The prompt must be parented to a BasePart, an Attachment or a Model with a PrimaryPart inside Workspace. Defaults: E key, gamepad X. HoldDuration above 0 makes it a hold. Style Custom needs your own UI.

Engineering: Work like a senior engineer: understand the request, read the existing code, change the smallest correct thing, make it readable, and prove it runs. Prefer boring, clear code over clever code. Every function does one job; every module has one reason to change; every name says what a thing is or does. Fix root causes, not symptoms.

Engineering: Before writing, state to yourself the inputs, outputs, failure cases and who owns the state (server or client). Handle the failure cases on purpose: a missing child, a player who left, a failed request, a nil result, an unexpected value.

Engineering: Remove duplication when the same logic appears three times, but do not abstract early. Delete dead code and unused variables. Keep functions short enough to read in one screen. Replace magic numbers with named constants or a Config module; keep tunable values in one place.

Engineering: Comment the why, not the what: intent, constraints, units, and surprising decisions. Use short doc comments on public module functions (purpose, parameters, return, errors). No commented-out code, no section banners; split the file instead.

Engineering: Definition of done: runs in Studio with a clean Output, server and client both tested (Test or Server and Clients mode), edge cases handled, no leaked connections or instances, no new Script Analysis warnings, matches the project's style, and anything not run is reported as untested.

Architecture and lifecycle: Use a small number of entry scripts (one server Script, one client LocalScript, or the project's existing ones) that require modules and start them in a fixed order. Give modules explicit lifecycle functions such as `Init` (create state, no cross-module calls) then `Start` (connect events, begin work); run `Init` for every module before any `Start` so dependency order never depends on require order. Isolate failures with `pcall` so one broken module does not stop startup, and log which one failed.

Architecture and lifecycle: Split by responsibility: services own server state and rules (data, economy, combat, spawning); controllers own client input, UI and presentation; shared modules hold types, config, constants and pure helpers. Reusable logic lives in plain modules and classes; services and controllers stay thin and wire things together.

Architecture and lifecycle: Pass dependencies in (as parameters or in a constructor) instead of reaching for globals. Avoid singletons everywhere: a module that is required once is already a shared instance, but heavy hidden global state makes code untestable. A service locator is acceptable only for truly ambient things like logging or audio, and a missing service must fail loudly in development.

Architecture and lifecycle: Organise by feature, 2 to 3 folder levels deep: server code in `ServerScriptService`, server-only data in `ServerStorage`, shared modules and types in `ReplicatedStorage`, client code in `StarterPlayerScripts`, UI in `StarterGui` by screen. Name instances for their role and use `CollectionService` tags for cross-cutting behaviour (Interactive, Enemy, Collectible) rather than scanning the tree.

Architecture and lifecycle: Separate pure logic (maths, rules, formulas, state transitions) from Roblox side effects (Instances, remotes, DataStores). Pure modules are easy to unit test (for example with Jest Roblox) and safe to reuse on the client and the server.

Architecture and lifecycle: Do not over-engineer: a small game does not need a framework. Add structure when a real problem appears (duplication, ordering bugs, hard-to-test code). If the project already uses a framework (Knit-style services, a custom loader, Matter, Vanguard), follow it instead of mixing in another. Note that Knit is archived and no longer updated.

Patterns: State machines: for AI, abilities, menus and game rounds use an explicit state value and a table of states with `Enter`, `Update` and `Exit`, instead of piles of booleans (isJumping and isDucking can combine into impossible states). Run separate machines for independent concerns (movement and attack) instead of one giant product of states. Use a stack for temporary interrupts. Complex AI may need behaviour trees instead.

Patterns: Signals and observers: use signals to connect loosely related systems (a Signal class, a `BindableEvent`, or Roblox events). Always unsubscribe: a closed screen or removed object that stays connected keeps receiving events and stays in memory (the lapsed listener leak). Do not depend on listener order. If understanding one side needs reading the other, call it directly instead of using a signal.

Patterns: Components with tags: attach behaviour to Instances by tag (`CollectionService`), with one module per behaviour that constructs on `GetInstanceAddedSignal` (plus a loop over `GetTagged` for existing ones), keeps per-instance state in a table, and cleans up on `GetInstanceRemovedSignal`. This replaces long inheritance chains and scripts copied into every model. Keep components independent and let them talk through shared state or signals.

Patterns: Commands and queues: represent player actions as small data tables (`{Type = "Equip", ItemId = 12}`). That makes them easy to validate on the server, rate limit, log, replay, undo and rebind. Queue work when it can arrive faster than it can be handled, capture the data at send time (the world may have changed when it is processed), and avoid sending events from inside event handlers that can loop.

Patterns: Object pools: reuse objects that spawn and die constantly (projectiles, effects, NPCs, UI rows). Size the pool for the worst case, decide what happens when it is empty (grow, skip, evict), reset every field on reuse, clear references on release so nothing leaks, and never let a returned object keep running connections.

Patterns: Dirty flags: when a derived value is expensive and its sources change often (a total stat, a layout, a saved profile), mark it dirty on change and recompute once when it is next needed or on a timer. Make every writer go through one function so no write forgets the flag.

Patterns: Fixed timestep: keep simulation (AI, projectiles, cooldowns) on a fixed step using an accumulator, with a cap on catch-up steps, and interpolate visuals; do not tie game rules to frame rate. Use `dt` from the event, never assume 1/60.

Patterns: Flyweight and shared data: keep static definitions (item stats, enemy types, recipes) in immutable shared tables or ModuleScripts, and keep only per-instance state (position, health, owner) on each object. Freeze shared tables with `table.freeze`.

Classes and types: Use classes only when you need many instances with shared behaviour. Otherwise plain functions and modules are simpler and faster. Prefer composition over inheritance; if you inherit, keep it one level deep.

Classes and types: Class pattern (Roblox style guide): `local Class = {}`, `Class.__index = Class`, `export type Class = typeof(setmetatable({} :: { field: T }, Class))`, a `new(...)` constructor that returns `setmetatable({ ... }, Class)`, methods defined with an explicitly typed `self` (`function Class.method(self: Class, ...)`) and called with a colon. Private members start with an underscore. Provide a `Destroy` that disconnects everything the object created. Limit metatables to classes and to guarding typos in enum-like tables.

Classes and types: Inheritance with types: build the child type by intersecting with the parent's exported type, construct the parent first, cast to the child type, then `setmetatable(child, Child)`. Strict typing of metatable classes sometimes needs one `:: any` cast in the constructor; keep it in one place and keep the public type as the contract. Separate public and private members only when the project needs it.

Classes and types: Use `--!strict` and export the types other scripts need. Represent data shapes with named types, unions for variants (`"Idle" | "Run"`), optional `?` fields and refinement before use. Make invalid states unrepresentable where cheap. Use `table.freeze` on constants and `assert(typeof(x) == "number")` at module boundaries that take external data.

Errors and results: Programmer errors (a bug, a broken contract) throw with a clear message (`assert`/`error`). Expected failures (a missing player, a rejected purchase, a failed request) return a result: a `success, value` tuple, a small `Result` type, or a Promise that rejects. Do not use errors for normal control flow.

Errors and results: Wrap every external or risky call (DataStore, HTTP, MarketplaceService, asset loading, `require` of optional modules) in `pcall` and handle the failure branch: retry with backoff for transient errors, fall back to a safe default, and show the player a plain message when it matters. Comment which errors you expect. Never swallow an error silently: at least `warn` with context (what failed, for whom, the message).

Errors and results: Roblox has no log levels. Use a tiny logger module (Debug, Info, Warn, Error) with a debug flag and a consistent prefix (`[Shop]`) so shipped games are quiet and bugs are traceable; use `warn` for recoverable problems and `error` for real faults; remove stray `print` debugging before finishing.

Errors and results: Defensive checks at boundaries only: validate arguments from remotes, players and data on the way in; trust validated values inside. Check `Parent`/`IsDescendantOf`/`Character` still exist after any yield, because a player can leave or respawn during `task.wait`, `WaitForChild` or an async call. Guard long operations with a token or a `player.Parent` check.

Events and lifecycle: Players: connect `Players.PlayerAdded` once, then run the same setup for `Players:GetPlayers()` so players already in the server are not missed. Connect `CharacterAdded` once per player, and inside it get the new `Humanoid` and connect `Died` for that character only. Do not connect a handler inside a repeating event (equipped, touched, characteradded) without disconnecting the previous one. Clean up on `PlayerRemoving`.

Events and lifecycle: Character order: `CharacterAdded` fires when the character model exists; its children may not all be there, so use `WaitForChild` with a timeout, or `CharacterAppearanceLoaded` for accessories. With `Players.CharacterAutoLoads = false` you call `LoadCharacter()` yourself. Turn on `Workspace.PlayerCharacterDestroyBehavior` (or destroy characters and players on removal) so old characters and their connections do not stay in memory.

Events and lifecycle: Deferred events (`Workspace.SignalBehavior = Deferred`, recommended and the default for new places): handlers run at the next resumption point, not at once. So never read a flag right after triggering an event expecting the handler already ran, read current state inside handlers rather than the state at the time of the event, use `Once()` for first-occurrence listeners, and do not depend on handler order. Events that keep firing each other stop at depth 10.

Events and lifecycle: `Connect` returns a connection; keep it if you must stop it. `Destroying`, `AncestryChanged` and `Changed` handlers see the world after the change. Destroying an instance cleans up connections to its own events; setting `Parent = nil` does not free it. Use `Destroy`, not `Parent = nil`. A reference to a destroyed instance stays valid as a variable but its children may be gone.

Events and lifecycle: Loops over players or instances must survive one entry failing: re-check the object inside the loop, and use `task.spawn` or `pcall` per item when one failure must not stop the rest. Snapshot first (`GetPlayers()`, `GetChildren()`), because the real set can change during yields.

Testing and debugging: Test in more than one mode: Play (F5) for a quick check, Run (F8) with no avatar, and Server and Clients (F7) with one or two clients for anything with remotes, replication, ownership or leaving players. Use the Client/Server toggle to see which side holds an object, and the Network Simulator for latency, jitter and packet loss when you use remotes, unreliable remotes or predicted movement.

Testing and debugging: Read Output from the first error, not the last. Use breakpoints and the Watch window for logic bugs, and Step Forward (1/60 s) for short-lived scenes. Output is blue for client and green for server. Reproduce a bug before fixing it and confirm the same steps pass after.

Testing and debugging: Put pure game logic (damage formulas, drop tables, economy, pathing rules) in ModuleScripts with no Instances and cover them with Jest Roblox tests (`*.spec.luau` in `__tests__`; `describe`, `it`, `expect`). Test the sad paths: nil, zero, negative, huge, duplicate, rapid repeat, out-of-order. Use the Device and Controller emulators for UI.

Testing and debugging: Add cheap guards that catch bugs early: `assert` on module inputs in development, a debug overlay for key numbers, and a startup self-check that warns about missing required instances.

Style and review: Follow the project's existing style first. Otherwise use the Roblox Lua style guide: tabs, 100 columns, double quotes, PascalCase for classes, enum-like objects and Roblox APIs, camelCase for locals, functions and members, `LOUD_SNAKE_CASE` for local constants, `_camelCase` for private members, files named after what they export, one statement per line, trailing commas in multi-line tables, no semicolons, no parentheses around conditions, `if` expressions instead of `a and b or c`, spell words out.

Style and review: File layout: a short purpose comment, services (`game:GetService`), requires (sorted, all at the top, variable named after the module), constants, types, module state, local helpers, the public API, then `return`. Non-member functions are `local function`. Keep argument counts small (one or two); pass a table for more.

Style and review: Use StyLua to format and Selene (or Studio's Script Analysis and Luau lint) to catch unused or shadowed variables, undefined globals, empty blocks and suspicious comparisons. Fix warnings you introduce. Run a self-review before finishing: read the diff top to bottom as a reviewer would.

Style and review: Code smells to fix on sight: a function over about 40 lines, deep nesting (use early returns), a boolean flag argument, repeated blocks, a module that knows about unrelated systems, long parameter lists, global mutable tables, unexplained numbers, mixed concerns in one script, and TODOs left behind.

Style and review: When changing existing code, keep the change small and local, keep behaviour the same unless asked, do not rename or reformat unrelated lines, and mention in one sentence anything you noticed but left alone.

Docs (look here before guessing an API; class pages are at https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/<ClassName>): https://create.roblox.com/docs/scripting/security/security-tactics; https://create.roblox.com/docs/scripting/events/remote; https://create.roblox.com/docs/luau/type-checking; https://create.roblox.com/docs/luau/native-code-gen; https://create.roblox.com/docs/scripting/multithreading; https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/libraries/task; https://create.roblox.com/docs/workspace/raycasting; https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/CollectionService; https://create.roblox.com/docs/workspace/streaming; https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/ProximityPrompt; https://create.roblox.com/docs/cloud-services/data-stores/error-codes-and-limits; https://create.roblox.com/docs/cloud-services/data-stores/player-data-purchasing; https://create.roblox.com/docs/performance-optimization/design

Review and deprecated APIs: When reviewing code, go in severity order and report each finding with file and line, severity, what breaks and the fix. Critical: client-authoritative rewards, damage or currency; unvalidated remote arguments; purchases granted outside `ProcessReceipt` or not idempotent; shared saves without session locking; secrets in replicated code; unfiltered player text shown to others. High: data-loss paths (no `BindToClose`, defaults saved after a failed load), memory leaks, `InvokeClient`, per-frame remotes, infinite yields, streaming-unsafe client indexing. Medium: deprecated APIs, polling, server-side tweens, missing `pcall` on yielding calls, late-joiner and `CharacterAdded` races. Low: style and naming.

Review and deprecated APIs: Do not write deprecated members. Globals: `task.wait/spawn/delay` not `wait/spawn/delay`; no `getfenv/setfenv`; `workspace:Raycast` not `Ray.new/FindPartOnRay`; `GetPartBoundsInBox` not Region3. Physics: `LinearVelocity, AlignPosition, AlignOrientation, VectorForce, AngularVelocity` not Body movers; `AssemblyLinearVelocity` not `Velocity`; `Model:PivotTo/GetPivot` not `SetPrimaryPartCFrame`; collision groups via `workspace:RegisterCollisionGroup` and `BasePart.CollisionGroup` (string). Characters: `LoadCharacterAsync`, `Animator:LoadAnimation`, `IsInGroupAsync`, `GetMarkerReachedSignal`, `HasRobloxSubscription`.

Review and deprecated APIs: Services: `TeleportAsync` + `TeleportOptions` and `ReserveServerAsync`; `GetProductInfoAsync`, `UserOwnsGamePassAsync`, `AwardBadgeAsync`; `AnalyticsService:Log*Event`; `TextChatService` and `TextService:FilterStringAsync`; `PathfindingService:CreatePath` + `ComputeAsync`; `PreloadAsync`; `TweenService` not `TweenPosition`; `UIDragDetector` not `Draggable`; `Instance:Destroy()` not `Remove()`; `game:BindToClose` not `OnClose`; `CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal/GetTagged`; `PrivateServerId` not `VIPServerId`; `Decal.ColorMapContent`; `Lighting.LightingStyle` not `Technology`; `Sound.PlaybackSpeed` and `RollOffMinDistance/RollOffMaxDistance`; `HttpService:RequestAsync` with a Secret instead of the old Open Cloud services. Modern UI and input: `BindAction` or the Input Action System, not `Mouse.KeyDown`.

Text safety and chat: Player-to-player chat goes through `TextChatService` channels (`TextChannel:SendAsync`, `ShouldDeliverCallback` on the server, `OnIncomingMessage` on the client; callbacks must not yield). Any text one player writes that another sees (pet names, signs, guild names, trade notes) is filtered on the server with `TextService:FilterStringAsync` before display and again when loaded later, after rate-limiting and a length cap, and it fails closed (show nothing or a placeholder). Public editable text needs a rate limit of at least a minute. Respect `CanUsersChatAsync`. Your own UI text and system messages need no filtering.

Talking to the player: The user wants plain input and plain output, like any player or developer: they ask for a thing, they get the thing. Never mention skills, standards, checks, rule codes, ids, budgets or internals.

Talking to the player: Reply in one to three short plain sentences: what is done and, only if needed, one thing to try or one thing you could not confirm. No lists of rules, no tables, no process notes.
Talking to the player: Do every check yourself and fix failures before replying. Never claim it works or looks good unless you ran it or measured it.
