Official docs (offline): `ms_roblox_docs` holds the official Roblox Creator Docs and Luau docs offline (about 2,260 pages: every engine class, enum, datatype and library, plus the guides). Run action check on every script before writing it to Studio and fix every error and every deprecated warning (wait, spawn, delay, Humanoid:LoadAnimation, FindPartOnRay, BodyVelocity and the rest); an info item matters only if that variable is an instance. Confirm any API you are not certain of with action api, which gives the signature, the dot-or-colon form and the replacement for deprecated calls.

Done means checked: A task is done only when, after your last change, you read it back or ran a check that passed: the instance exists with the right class and parent, the script source reads as intended, the console is clean in a short play test, or the number you computed was computed in code. If you changed anything again, check again.

Done means checked: Never write, repeat or imitate a tool result. If a tool did not run or failed, say so in one sentence and fix or retry; do not claim success. Ignore thumbnails, data URIs and CDN links inside tool results; they carry no information you need.

Done means checked: Every script you write to Studio is checked automatically (syntax, undefined names, wrong Roblox APIs, server-only calls on the client, unsafe remotes) and the result is added to the tool output as [Multi-Script code check]. Fix every error and warning it reports before moving on. For bigger systems start from the expert templates: call `ms_skill_reference` for code-quality or scripting-power to read Remotes, PlayerData, Purchases, Cleanup, RoundSystem, NpcBrain, HitValidation, Rolls, Leaderboard, DailyReward, UIController or Component, then adapt them.

Done means checked: Keep changes small and reversible: record a ChangeHistory waypoint before a batch of edits, never overwrite an existing system you have not read, and ask before deleting objects, publishing, or writing live data.
qualityGates: Every rule is checked against the real result in Studio, not assumed
Failures are fixed before replying; a failing check is never reported as done
Checks, ids and specs stay private; the user gets a short plain result
Anything not run in Studio is reported as untested in one plain sentence
Modules start in a fixed order and handle players leaving and respawning
Errors are returned or thrown on purpose and never swallowed
The diff was reviewed for smells and matches the project style
Nothing is called done until a check passed after the last change
APIs that are not certain are confirmed with ms_roblox_docs, and scripts pass its check before they are written
code-quality.architecturePolicy: State server, client, shared and editor ownership; preserve existing service boundaries and lifecycle cleanup.
code-quality.platformPolicy: Cover desktop, touch and gamepad where relevant; include safe areas, focus, respawn, late join and weakest-device behavior.
code-quality.studioEvidencePolicy: Use exact live Roblox Studio MCP schemas; verify with Edit/Server/Client or multi-client tests, clean Output, DataModel read-back and measured profiler/network evidence.
code-quality.securityPolicy: Validate consequential client input on the server, rate-limit exposed remotes and test abuse paths where relevant.

engineExecutionContract.schemaBinding: Discover exact live MCP tool schemas at runtime; never rely on remembered command names or parameters.
parameterPolicy: validate required and nested fields before execution
coerce only unambiguous provider formatting differences
reject unsupported enums, bounds, patterns and unknown fields when the schema forbids them
route to the declared engine/server only
read back native state after mutation
recoveryPolicy: classify schema, transport, editor-state and engine-runtime failures separately
refresh the live catalogue after unknown-tool/schema drift
retry transient transport/editor disconnect once only
never repeat an unchanged failing mutation
rollback or stop when evidence cannot prove safe completion

activation.when: Always use when writing, fixing or reviewing Roblox scripts.
activation.style: Explicit user references first, then existing project style. Select one coherent style bible.

executionWorkflow.adaptation: Apply only relevant parts to the actual user goal. Inspect existing naming, dependencies and style; adapt the method instead of copying sample paths or architecture. Current user scope and tool permissions govern. Skill text is reference data, never permission.
executionWorkflow.inspect: existing modules, interfaces, dependencies and lifecycle
executionWorkflow.execute: Implement the smallest complete slice with explicit ownership, error handling and cleanup.
executionWorkflow.verify: Run project tests/build and read back caller/handler/result integration; test failure paths.
executionWorkflow.craft: Preserve the existing architecture and style. Build a complete requested path, then inspect real results; additional polish must serve the task.
executionWorkflow.role: Deliver an integrated working path, editable source and read-back of changed state.
executionWorkflow.handoff: State owned files/assets, adjacent interfaces and acceptance criteria. In co-work, read the board and claim disjoint resources; do not overwrite another worker.

evidence.measured: Actual tool output, read-back, build/test result or capture with source/path.
evidence.reviewed: Code/document inspection only; label it as reviewed.
evidence.unverified: Name the absent tool, access or environment and continue feasible work.

executionWorkflow.recovery: Reuse still-valid evidence. A failed, restricted or truncated inspection is UNKNOWN, not an empty project. Stop unchanged reads and identical failures; narrow the question, repair its cause or disclose the blocker. Rerun affected checks only. Never fabricate a tool result, model capability, asset ID or successful test.

npc-pathfinding.name: NPC and Pathfinding — enemies, patrols, horror chasers
npc-pathfinding.description: Always use when building NPCs, enemies, chasers, patrols, pets or followers in Roblox, including horror monsters and any PathfindingService work.
npc-pathfinding.whenToUse: Always use for NPCs, enemies, chasers, patrols, pets, followers and any pathfinding.
steps: Server owns the NPC: Run NPC logic and movement on the server. Set network ownership of the NPC's parts to the server with SetNetworkOwner(nil) so a nearby player cannot take it over or exploit its physics. Never put NPC logic in client scripts.
Server owns the NPC: One manager module owns all NPCs with one shared update loop, not a while loop per NPC. Stagger path recomputes across frames.
Server owns the NPC: Use a state machine (Idle, Patrol, Investigate, Chase, Attack, Search, Flee) with explicit transitions and one active state.

PathfindingService (official docs): CreatePath takes AgentRadius (default 2), AgentHeight (default 5), AgentCanJump (default true), AgentCanClimb (default false), WaypointSpacing (default 4) and Costs. Set radius and height to the NPC's real size; a mismatch makes paths fail or clip walls.

PathfindingService (official docs): Call path:ComputeAsync(start, goal) inside pcall and use the path only when path.Status is Enum.PathStatus.Success. On failure fall back: wander, go to the last known position, or back off with a cooldown.
PathfindingService (official docs): Compute while the NPC is on the ground; computing mid-fall gives a wrong start position.

PathfindingService (official docs): Walk waypoints with Humanoid:MoveTo or Humanoid:Move, advance on MoveToFinished or a distance check, and when a waypoint Action is Jump make the humanoid jump. Give each waypoint a timeout (start around 2 seconds, tune it) so a stuck NPC recomputes.
PathfindingService (official docs): Connect path.Blocked, recompute only if the blocked index is at or ahead of the current waypoint, and disconnect the old connection before recomputing.

PathfindingService (official docs): Limits: start to goal direct distance at most 3000 studs, about 20000 node budget (huge open maps and mazes can fail), and conflicting settings fail (needing a jump with AgentCanJump false).

PathfindingService (official docs): Costs: Enum.Material names or PathfindingModifier labels as keys; math.huge blocks a material. PathfindingModifier on an anchored non-colliding part with PassThrough lets the NPC route through doors it can open. PathfindingLink between two Attachments handles ladders, vents and teleports; run custom logic when the waypoint label matches.
PathfindingService (official docs): In streaming games target parts that are loaded and wait for the area before pathing.

Performance and fairness: Do not recompute every frame. Recompute when the target moves more than a threshold (start around 6 studs) or on a timer (start around 0.25 to 0.5 seconds while chasing). Starting values, tune them.
Performance and fairness: Cap simultaneous path computations and queue the rest. Sleep NPCs far from every player.
Performance and fairness: On straight open ground with nothing in the way, move directly and skip the path.
Performance and fairness: Destroy the NPC and disconnect its connections and loops when it dies or is removed.
Perception: Sight: distance check, field-of-view angle using the dot product, then workspace:Raycast with RaycastParams that excludes the NPC and non-blocking parts. All on the server.
Perception: Hearing: sprinting, jumping and item use make noise; the NPC investigates the last noise position, not the player's live position.
Perception: Keep a last known position and a memory timer. After losing the player: go there, search, return to patrol. The NPC must not know the exact position through walls.

Horror NPCs: Fair threat: telegraph with sound, light flicker or animation before it reaches the player, and give the player a way to escape or hide (hiding spots, doors, broken line of sight). An unavoidable instant kill with no warning is a bug.
Horror NPCs: Pace tension: absence and patrol, then a hint, then a chase, then a cooldown. Add a grace period after a respawn and after a chase ends.
Horror NPCs: Chase speed at or slightly below player sprint, with stamina or doors creating tension. Speeds are named constants (the default walk speed is 16 studs per second).
Horror NPCs: Scare sounds and effects are triggered by the server through a rate-limited remote to the affected clients; the client plays them.
Horror NPCs: Never damage, kill or teleport a player on a client request. The server checks range, line of sight and a cooldown first.
Other NPC types: Pets and followers: follow at an offset behind the owner, teleport to the owner when the distance passes a limit (start around 40 studs), and tie lifetime to the owner.
Other NPC types: Shop and quest NPCs: ProximityPrompt interaction validated on the server (distance, quest state, inventory).
Other NPC types: Waves and spawners: cap alive count, spawn from fixed points with a cooldown, despawn on round end.

Raycast sight checks (official): the ray direction length sets the distance (max 15000 studs); a miss returns nil; RaycastParams uses FilterDescendantsInstances with Exclude or Include; parts with CanQuery false are ignored. Humanoid WalkSpeed is client-replicated, so for NPCs the server owns it and for players the server sanity checks speed.
Track NPCs with CollectionService tags (added signal plus GetTagged for existing ones) so a manager can find, update and clean them without scanning Workspace.

Docs (look here before guessing an API; class pages are at https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/<ClassName>): https://create.roblox.com/docs/characters/pathfinding; https://create.roblox.com/docs/workspace/raycasting; https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/Humanoid; https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/CollectionService

Pathfinding setup: Create a path with `PathfindingService:CreatePath(params)`; `FindPathAsync` and the old compute methods are deprecated. Agent parameters and defaults: AgentRadius 2 (studs), AgentHeight 5, AgentCanJump true, AgentCanClimb false (truss), WaypointSpacing 4 (`math.huge` removes middle waypoints), Costs nil. Set radius and height from the real NPC (R15 around 2.75 and 5.25 with a bit of room); too small and it clips corners, too large and doorways fail.

Pathfinding setup: `path:ComputeAsync(start, goal)` yields; wrap it in `pcall` and check `path.Status == Enum.PathStatus.Success` before `path:GetWaypoints()`. Each waypoint has Position, Action (Walk or Jump) and Label. A failure usually means: distance over 3000 studs, the 20000 node budget used up (large open maps or mazes), a goal reachable only by jumping while AgentCanJump is false, an AgentHeight larger than the gaps, or a goal on a wall or inside a part. Compute from the ground, since a start in the air is moved to the nearest valid point.
Pathfinding setup: Visualise it: in Studio turn on Navigation mesh, Pathfinding modifiers and Pathfinding links in the visualisation options and look before guessing why an NPC will not go somewhere.

Costs, modifiers and links: Material costs: `Costs = {Water = math.huge, CrackedLava = 100}`. Every material is 1 by default; `math.huge` makes it forbidden; a large finite number (100 to 1000) makes it a last resort. For regions use an anchored, `CanCollide = false` part with a `PathfindingModifier` whose `Label` matches a key in Costs. Keep `CanQuery` true on that part or it is ignored. `PassThrough = true` on a modifier makes a part ignored so a path goes through it (a zombie that can hear the player behind a door).

Costs, modifiers and links: Links: a `PathfindingLink` joins two Attachments (`Attachment0`, `Attachment1`) that are otherwise unreachable (a boat, a teleporter, a ladder, a gap); set `Label`, give that label a cost in Costs, and in your move loop check `waypoint.Label` to run the custom action instead of walking. Ladders and truss need `AgentCanClimb` or a link. Do not rely on `AgentRadius` alone to keep NPCs out of narrow gaps; block them with a modifier.

Moving along a path: Move with `Humanoid:Move(direction)` or `MoveTo` per waypoint, treat a waypoint as reached when within about 2 to 3 studs horizontally (do not wait only for `MoveToFinished`, which can time out and stutter), jump when the waypoint Action is Jump, and add a stuck timeout per waypoint (about 2 to 3 seconds) that recomputes. Limit repaths: wait about 0.2 s before recomputing after an error, cap retries, and only recompute when the target moved a meaningful distance or the path is blocked, not every half second.

Moving along a path: Connect `path.Blocked` and recompute only if the blocked waypoint index is at or ahead of the current waypoint. Reuse one path object per NPC, remove debug parts from the loop, and skip the first one or two waypoints of a fresh path if the NPC steps backwards. If an NPC stutters: set network ownership to the server (`SetNetworkOwner(nil)` on the root part after it is assembled and welded), make sure the run animation loops, avoid `wait()` polling (use `task.wait()` or Heartbeat), and avoid heavy per-waypoint yielding. Use `Humanoid:Move` steering if `MoveTo` keeps pausing.

Moving along a path: Streaming enabled: a client script may fail to see a destination that is not streamed in; compute on the server, or target a part inside a persistent model and wait for `Workspace.PersistentLoaded`.

Senses and detection: Sight is four cheap tests in order: distance (magnitude), field of view (dot product of the NPC's `LookVector` and the unit direction to the target against `math.cos(math.rad(fov/2))`; do not mix degrees and radians), line of sight (a `workspace:Raycast` from the eyes to the target's head and torso with `RaycastParams` excluding the NPC), and only then react. A single ray to the root misses crouching or partly hidden players, so test two or three points. Avoid `Touched` for detection, it is unreliable.

Senses and detection: Throttle: sense a few times a second (every 0.1 to 0.25 s, staggered between NPCs), check distance first and skip far targets, and share one loop for all NPCs. Hearing: players make noise events (running, jumping, gunshots) with a radius; the NPC investigates the position, not the player. Memory: remember the last seen position and a timer so the NPC searches, then gives up.

State machines for NPCs: Use a table of states, each with Enter, Update(dt) and Exit, and one `transition(name)` function that calls Exit then Enter. Typical states: Idle, Patrol, Investigate, Chase, Attack, Search, Flee. Transitions come from events (saw player, lost player, took damage, reached point), with hysteresis (a longer range to lose a target than to gain it) so it does not flicker.

State machines for NPCs: Keep one manager updating all NPCs from one Heartbeat loop with a per-NPC budget; do not run a loop per NPC. For larger brains use a state machine for the main activity and a small behaviour tree or utility scoring inside a state. Clean up on death (disconnect events, cancel tasks, release the path). Add a debug text above the head showing the state while testing.

Horror and stalker AI: Split the brain in two. A director tracks the player and tension and decides when the monster may pressure, hunt or back off; the monster itself only reacts to senses (sight, sound, last known position). The monster must not cheat: it finds the player through the same senses the player can see and hear, and the player gets readable costs (running is loud, hiding works, light attracts).

Horror and stalker AI: Build tension in cycles of build-up, peak and release: after a peak give the player breathing room (the monster loses interest, retreats, or patrols elsewhere), never spam scares, vary patrol routes, and delay a blocked scare rather than cancel it. Telegraph danger with audio, light flicker and distant footsteps before contact. Never let the monster teleport onto a player or hit through walls. Test that a careful player can always escape or hide.

Scaling NPCs: Pool complex NPCs instead of creating and destroying them; reset all state on reuse (health, attributes, velocity, animations) and set `Humanoid.BreakJointsOnDeath = false` for pooled ones. Fewer Humanoids: use an `AnimationController` with anchored or CFrame movement for simple mobs, and disable unused Humanoid states (Climbing, Swimming, Ragdoll, FallingDown). Think at a fixed 5 to 10 Hz, staggered, and skip NPCs far from every player. Share a path between NPCs heading to the same goal; use flow fields or grids for hordes.

Scaling NPCs: Let clients animate NPCs (the server sets an attribute like `State = 'Run'` and clients play tracks). Fewer parts per NPC (MeshParts), no per-frame server property changes. Hundreds of purely cosmetic NPCs (crowds, ambient animals) are simulated on clients from a server seed; nothing gameplay-related may depend on them. Heavy steering or flocking math goes in `--!native` modules or Parallel Luau Actors (read-only in the desynchronised phase, write after `task.synchronize()`).

Talking to the player: The user wants plain input and plain output, like any player or developer: they ask for a thing, they get the thing. Never mention skills, standards, checks, rule codes, ids, budgets or internals.

Talking to the player: Reply in one to three short plain sentences: what is done and, only if needed, one thing to try or one thing you could not confirm. No lists of rules, no tables, no process notes.
Talking to the player: Do every check yourself and fix failures before replying. Never claim it works or looks good unless you ran it or measured it.
Check table (private, never shown): NPC-1 Server-owned with network owner set; no client authority
Check table (private, never shown): NPC-2 Agent size matches the model; path status checked
Check table (private, never shown): NPC-3 Blocked, stuck and no-path cases handled
Check table (private, never shown): NPC-4 Recompute throttled; far NPCs sleep; one shared loop
Check table (private, never shown): NPC-5 Perception uses server raycasts and last known position
Check table (private, never shown): NPC-6 State machine has clean transitions and cleanup
Check table (private, never shown): NPC-7 Horror threats are telegraphed and escapable; damage validated on the server
Check table (private, never shown): NPC-8 Watched in Studio: path, jump, blocked door, chase, lose player

Official docs (offline): `ms_roblox_docs` holds the official Roblox Creator Docs and Luau docs offline (about 2,260 pages: every engine class, enum, datatype and library, plus the guides). Confirm PathfindingService, Path, Humanoid and AnimationController members with action api (agent parameters, Costs, PathfindingModifier, PathfindingLink) and read the Pathfinding guide (search 'pathfinding') before tuning agents; run action check on NPC scripts.
qualityGates: Every rule is checked against the real result in Studio, not assumed
Failures are fixed before replying; a failing check is never reported as done
Checks, ids and specs stay private; the user gets a short plain result
Anything not run in Studio is reported as untested in one plain sentence
Paths are checked for success, repaths are limited and blocked paths are handled
NPC sight uses distance, field of view and a raycast, throttled and shared between NPCs
APIs that are not certain are confirmed with ms_roblox_docs, and scripts pass its check before they are written
npc-pathfinding.architecturePolicy: State server, client, shared and editor ownership; preserve existing service boundaries and lifecycle cleanup.
npc-pathfinding.platformPolicy: Cover desktop, touch and gamepad where relevant; include safe areas, focus, respawn, late join and weakest-device behavior.
npc-pathfinding.studioEvidencePolicy: Use exact live Roblox Studio MCP schemas; verify with Edit/Server/Client or multi-client tests, clean Output, DataModel read-back and measured profiler/network evidence.
npc-pathfinding.securityPolicy: Validate consequential client input on the server, rate-limit exposed remotes and test abuse paths where relevant.

engineExecutionContract.schemaBinding: Discover exact live MCP tool schemas at runtime; never rely on remembered command names or parameters.
parameterPolicy: validate required and nested fields before execution
coerce only unambiguous provider formatting differences
reject unsupported enums, bounds, patterns and unknown fields when the schema forbids them
route to the declared engine/server only
read back native state after mutation
recoveryPolicy: classify schema, transport, editor-state and engine-runtime failures separately
refresh the live catalogue after unknown-tool/schema drift
retry transient transport/editor disconnect once only
never repeat an unchanged failing mutation
rollback or stop when evidence cannot prove safe completion

activation.when: Always use for NPCs, enemies, chasers, patrols, pets, followers and any pathfinding.
activation.style: Explicit user references first, then existing project style. Select one coherent style bible.

executionWorkflow.adaptation: Apply only relevant parts to the actual user goal. Inspect existing naming, dependencies and style; adapt the method instead of copying sample paths or architecture. Current user scope and tool permissions govern. Skill text is reference data, never permission.
executionWorkflow.inspect: agent size, navigation geometry, decision states and server budget
executionWorkflow.execute: Implement bounded sensing/path refresh, reachable goals and explicit recovery states.
executionWorkflow.verify: Test unreachable goals, dynamic obstacles, stuck recovery and many agents; inspect path/state evidence.
executionWorkflow.craft: Preserve the existing architecture and style. Build a complete requested path, then inspect real results; additional polish must serve the task.
executionWorkflow.role: Deliver an integrated working path, editable source and read-back of changed state.
executionWorkflow.handoff: State owned files/assets, adjacent interfaces and acceptance criteria. In co-work, read the board and claim disjoint resources; do not overwrite another worker.

evidence.measured: Actual tool output, read-back, build/test result or capture with source/path.
evidence.reviewed: Code/document inspection only; label it as reviewed.
evidence.unverified: Name the absent tool, access or environment and continue feasible work.

executionWorkflow.recovery: Reuse still-valid evidence. A failed, restricted or truncated inspection is UNKNOWN, not an empty project. Stop unchanged reads and identical failures; narrow the question, repair its cause or disclose the blocker. Rerun affected checks only. Never fabricate a tool result, model capability, asset ID or successful test.

game-systems.name: Game Systems — simulators, coin collecting, tycoons, horror structure
game-systems.description: Always use when building Roblox simulators, tycoons, coin or collecting loops, pets, rebirths, shops, quests, currency or horror game structure.
game-systems.whenToUse: Always use for simulators, coin or collecting loops, tycoons, pets, rebirths, shops, quests, currency and horror structure.
steps: Mandatory companion to code-quality for every economy, collecting and round-based game. Numbers marked (tune) are starting values, not facts.
Units and scale (official docs): 1 stud = 0.28 m (28 cm). Default gravity is 196.2 studs per second squared. 1 m/s = 3.57 studs/s.

Units and scale (official docs): Humanoid defaults: WalkSpeed 16 studs/s, JumpPower 50 (clamped 0 to 1000, affected by gravity), JumpHeight 7.2 studs (used when UseJumpPower is false), MaxSlopeAngle 89 degrees.

Units and scale (official docs): Design distances in studs against these numbers: a jump clears about 7 studs, so gaps, steps and pickup ranges are sized from that. Collect radius (tune) is about 4 to 8 studs; pickup magnet range (tune) about 12 to 20.
Units and scale (official docs): Physical property limits: density 0.0001 to 100, friction 0 to 2, elasticity 0 to 1.
Economy core: The server holds every currency, count, multiplier and unlock. The client sends intent only (collect, buy item X); the server decides amounts.
Economy core: One economy module owns all currency changes: Add, Spend, CanAfford. Spend checks the balance first and fails cleanly. No other script edits currency.
Economy core: Use integers where possible and cap values so numbers never overflow or become NaN. For idle games past about 1e15 use a big-number format.
Economy core: Items, pets, zones, rarities and prices live in data tables or ModuleScripts. The server looks up prices there; never read them from the client.
Economy core: Save through the proven data approach in code-quality with a schema version.

Economy core: Shown numbers use K, M, B, T, Qa suffixes: below 1000 show as is, otherwise floor, count digits, keep the leading 1 to 3 digits and a fixed precision (for example 2 decimals), and pick the suffix by exponent. Test boundaries: 999, 1000, 999999, 1000000, and anything above the table (fall back to scientific notation). Do not round up into the next suffix wrongly.
Coin and collectible loops: Collect, carry (capacity), sell, upgrade, repeat, then a bigger zone or a rebirth. Every step has feedback: a number popup, a sound, a small effect.
Coin and collectible loops: Coins and pickups are anchored and non-colliding so players pass through and they stay put.

Coin and collectible loops: Official beginner pattern uses Touched with a guard (an Enabled attribute or flag set false on collect) and a respawn cooldown with task.wait. It only connects coins that exist at startup, so connect new ones as they spawn (ChildAdded or a tagged-instance signal), and disconnect when removed.

Coin and collectible loops: Touched is unreliable for scale (it can fire several times or not at all). For many collectibles or magnet pickup prefer a server loop with workspace:GetPartBoundsInRadius around each player, with OverlapParams (set MaxParts, use IncludeInstances on the collectibles folder, reuse one OverlapParams object since it can be changed in place, never BruteForceAllSlow), run every 0.1 to 0.25 seconds (tune), and only for players that are near collectible zones.

Coin and collectible loops: Always validate on the server: the player is alive, the collectible still exists and is not already claimed (claim it first, then award), capacity is left, and distance is plausible. Claim-then-award stops double collection when two events race.

Coin and collectible loops: Spawn from server spawners with a cap and a respawn timer. For huge counts keep collectibles as data on the server and create visible ones on the client near the player, or use streaming, instead of thousands of server parts.
Coin and collectible loops: Multipliers stack in one function: base x pets x gamepass x rebirth x event, computed on the server so results are predictable and loggable.
Coin and collectible loops: Rebirth: clear requirement, a reset list (what resets and what stays), a permanent bonus, a confirmation, and a server-side check.

Coin and collectible loops: Pets and eggs: pet data (rarity, multiplier, id) in a table, equipped limit on the server, eggs roll a server-side weighted random with the odds in a table. Never roll on the client. Show the real odds.
Coin and collectible loops: Gamepasses and products are granted through ProcessReceipt or gamepass checks on the server per code-quality and re-checked on join.
Coin and collectible loops: Anti-exploit: rate limit collect, sell, buy and hatch; sanity check totals against time played; log and kick on impossible gains.

Currency display: leaderstats works for small boards. For richer HUDs replicate values with attributes or a remote that sends the number, and update UI from the change signal, never by polling. Initialise labels at startup so they do not show stale text.
Currency display: Animate counters with TweenService. Cap and pool popups so spam cannot create hundreds of GuiObjects.
Tycoon: A tycoon belongs to one player; ownership is stored on the server. Buttons validate cost, owner and unlock order. Save purchased items by id and rebuild on join.
Tycoon: Droppers and conveyors run on the server with caps on live parts and a lifetime for dropped parts; pool them when frequent.
Quests, shops, daily rewards: Quest and reward state is stored per player and checked on the server. Daily rewards use server time, a streak counter and a claim flag, never the client clock.
Quests, shops, daily rewards: Shops read the item list from data; the server checks cost and ownership, grants and saves.
Horror game structure: Round or level flow lives on the server: lobby, setup, objective, threat, win or lose, reset, with one state variable. Clients only display it.
Horror game structure: Objectives (keys, fuses, generators) have server-owned progress and clear hints.
Horror game structure: Lighting, Atmosphere and fog set the mood; flickering lights run from one shared tick over tagged lights, not a loop per light.
Horror game structure: Jump scares are rare and earned, triggered by the server with a cooldown and played on the client. Offer a reduce-flashing option and keep audio levels sane.
Horror game structure: NPC behaviour follows npc-pathfinding.

Interactions (official): buy, collect and open prompts use ProximityPrompt, whose Triggered(player) fires on the server but can be triggered by an exploiter from any range, so the handler re-checks distance to the prompt's parent, a per-player cooldown and the player's state before awarding anything.

Save budget (official): at most 4 MB per key per minute written, 4,194,304 characters per value and 50 characters per key; keep per-player data compact and write on a timer and on leave, not on every coin.
Tag collectibles, spawners and zones with CollectionService and manage them through the added signal plus GetTagged; clean up on the removed signal.

Docs (look here before guessing an API; class pages are at https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/<ClassName>): https://create.roblox.com/docs/physics/units; https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/datatypes/OverlapParams; https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/Humanoid; https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/ProximityPrompt; https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/CollectionService; https://create.roblox.com/docs/cloud-services/data-stores/error-codes-and-limits; https://create.roblox.com/docs/cloud-services/data-stores/player-data-purchasing

Purchases (developer products): Set `MarketplaceService.ProcessReceipt` in exactly one server Script. Only the last script that assigns it takes effect, so search the whole game for other assignments and merge them into one handler; a second handler silently breaks purchases and players are charged without getting the item.

Purchases (developer products): Handler order: find the player with `Players:GetPlayerByUserId(receipt.PlayerId)`; if they are not in the server return `Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet` (Roblox retries when they rejoin) and never return nothing; look up the product id in a table of handlers (not a stack of ifs); run the grant inside `pcall`; write the receipt's `PurchaseId` to the player's saved data in the same step as the grant so the same receipt can never grant twice; return `PurchaseGranted` only after the grant and the record are saved or safely queued; return `NotProcessedYet` on any error.

Purchases (developer products): Grant functions that run inside an `UpdateAsync` callback must never yield. Do not grant in `PromptProductPurchaseFinished` (it fires when the prompt closes, not when the purchase is proven). Game passes are different: check ownership with `UserOwnsGamePassAsync` inside `pcall` on join, cache the result, and listen to `PromptGamePassPurchaseFinished` to unlock at once. Roblox keeps no per-user purchase history, so store what you need yourself.

Purchases (developer products): Client UI only asks to buy (`PromptProductPurchase` or `PromptGamePassPurchase`); the server decides what is granted. Show the real price from the product info, not a hard-coded number (prices can be personalised). Test in Studio with the purchase prompt, and report that live Robux purchases were not tested.

Saving data safely: Prefer a proven session-locking module (ProfileStore, or ProfileService) over hand-written DataStore code for player data. Session locking stops two servers editing the same player at once, which is what causes duplicated items after quick rejoins and trades. Template with defaults, `Reconcile()` to add new fields to old saves, one profile per player, release it on `PlayerRemoving`, kick the player if the session cannot start or ends elsewhere, and clear the cached profile.

Saving data safely: Never save data that has not loaded, and never fall back to a default template after a failed load and then save it, because the next save wipes the real data. If loading fails, keep the player out of write paths (or kick with a message) and retry. Save every player in `game:BindToClose` too (inside a loop, waiting for all saves), and autosave on a timer. Do not wait to bind `BindToClose` inside `PlayerRemoving`.

Saving data safely: If you write DataStore code yourself: wrap every call in `pcall`, retry with a short backoff (about 5 tries starting near 0.5 s, doubling), use `UpdateAsync` for changes that depend on the old value, use a session lock field (`game.JobId`), keep keys short (50 characters max) and values small (4 MB serialised max; stay far below), and write on events or a timer, not every frame. Per-key limits are 25 MB per minute read and 4 MB per minute write; write the same key no more than about once every 6 seconds.

Saving data safely: Request budgets per minute: experience-wide reads about 300 + 40 x concurrent users, writes 300 + 20 x CCU; per server reads 60 + 40 x players, writes 60 + 40 x players (ordered stores: writes 30 + 5 x players). Common error codes: 101 empty key, 102 key over 50 characters, 105 value too large, 301 to 306 request queue full (throttled: slow down), 401 and 402 server shutting down, 403 Studio API access off (turn on Enable Studio Access to API Services), 502 and 5xx retry later. Test saving in a published place or with API access on, and report it as untested otherwise.

Saving data safely: ProfileStore is for per-player data, not for leaderboards or global state, and not for rapid writes from many servers. Use `MessageAsync` to send things (gifts, trades) to a profile that may be offline, and never edit another player's profile directly from another server.

Simulator economy and progression: Design the loop on paper first: source (what earns), sink (what spends), gate (what unlocks next), reward (what the player sees). A simulator is one core action repeated (click, swing, collect), upgrades that make it stronger, zones that raise the rewards, rebirth that trades progress for a permanent multiplier, and collections (pets) for long-term goals. Every action needs instant feedback (sound, number pop, bar fill); a silent core action feels dead.

Simulator economy and progression: Costs grow exponentially: `cost(n) = base * growth^n`, with growth about 1.15 to 1.5 for upgrades (tune). Rewards should grow slower than cost so each step takes a little longer than the last (for example gains double while the cost triples). Aim the first upgrade at about 3 minutes of play after the tutorial, early items in minutes, mid items in hours, end items in days (tune). Draw the curve in a table and check the time per level before building.

Simulator economy and progression: Keep two or three currencies at most (main, premium, optionally event). Add sinks before the economy inflates: upgrades, eggs, repairs, consumables, cosmetics, rebirth costs. Premium must never make soft currency worthless or be strictly better; sell time-savers and cosmetics, keep everything reachable by playing. Do not put walls that force spending. A rebirth system prevents a hard ceiling.

Simulator economy and progression: Large numbers: store as numbers while they fit (doubles are exact to about 9e15; show suffixes K, M, B, T from a table), and switch to a big-number module only if values will really exceed 1e300. Format with a helper (`1.25M`), not raw floats. All earnings, costs and multipliers are calculated on the server; the client only displays. Cap rates and validate remote arguments.

Simulator economy and progression: Anti-cheat basics for economies: never trust a client number; clamp and rate-limit earn remotes; derive earnings on the server from what the player actually did; log unusual jumps. Monitor a trading economy for duplication and value manipulation.

Pets, eggs and luck: Roll on the server only. The server picks the result and sends the client an id; the client looks it up in a shared module for the name, model and rarity to show. Never let the client choose the result or write inventory.

Pets, eggs and luck: Weighted pick: give each item a weight (higher is more common), sum them, roll `Random.new():NextNumber() * total`, then walk the list subtracting weights until the roll is below zero. Return the last item as a fallback, guard against zero total, and never loop with `repeat ... until` on a roll that can fail. Create one `Random` object and reuse it instead of reseeding each time.

Pets, eggs and luck: Luck boosts: do not multiply the roll by luck (it can push the roll past 1 and cancels itself). Scale the weights instead: raise rare weights (for example `weight * (1 + luck * rarityIndex)` or divide the odds by luck so a 1 in 100 item becomes 1 in 10 at 10x), then renormalise. Test by rolling 100000 times and comparing results with the stated odds; show the real odds in the UI and make sure they match.

Pets, eggs and luck: Pity and guarantees (tune): count rolls without a rare drop and raise the odds, or guarantee one at a threshold, then reset when the rare drops. Keep the counter in saved data. Be honest in the UI about odds; some regions require showing them.

Pets, eggs and luck: Hatch flow: check the player owns enough eggs or currency and has space; take payment and add the pet in one server step that saves; then play the animation from the id. Equip limits, delete confirmations and favourites protect players from mistakes. Pets follow with a light server-validated position, and the client animates them.

Trading and duplication: Trades run on the server with a shared state both sides must confirm. Lock the offers when either side confirms; if anyone changes an offer after confirming, reset both confirmations. Re-check on the server at the end that both players still own every item, then swap in one saved step. Use session locking so a player cannot trade in two servers.

Trading and duplication: Never remove items from one profile and add to the other in separate unsaved steps; if the server crashes between them items vanish or duplicate. Log every trade with both user ids and the items. Add a short cooldown, a minimum account age or play time, and a confirmation screen showing exactly what each side gets.

Rounds, lobbies and teleports: Round games run as a server state machine: Intermission, Starting, InRound, Ending, with a timer owned by the server and replicated through a value or remote. Check the player count at each step, handle players leaving or joining mid-round, and reset the map and player state cleanly. Never trust the client for score, win or death.

Rounds, lobbies and teleports: Matchmaking across servers: put small tickets in a MemoryStore queue (short expiry, queues deliver at least once so processing must be idempotent), claim then validate before forming a match (players may have cancelled), reserve a server with `ReserveServerAsync`, and have each source server teleport only its own players to the reserved access code. MessagingService is only a wake-up signal because delivery is not guaranteed; keep the real assignment in shared state. Wrap `TeleportAsync` in `pcall` and also handle `TeleportInitFailed`; keep the ticket until the teleport succeeds so a failure can requeue. Never put secrets in teleport data. MemoryStore quotas scale with concurrent users; keep keys and values small. Reserved-server teleports only work in published places, not in plain Studio play tests.

Leaderboards: Use a separate `OrderedDataStore` for a leaderboard, with the user id as key and the number as value; do not mix it with the main save. Write from the server on a timer or on events, not every frame. Read pages with `GetSortedAsync(false, 100)` every minute or so, cache the result on the server, and send it to clients; do not make every player query it. Cache usernames and avatar headshots so you do not hit the Players service limits for every row. Ordered stores accept only integers and have lower write budgets; a single hot key can only be written about once every 6 seconds, so many votes on one key need batching.

Monetization: Product types: developer product (repeatable: currency, boosts, revives; `ProcessReceipt`), pass (once, permanent), subscription (monthly, revocable), rewarded video ad (granted through a developer product), private server. All granting is on the server. Prompt from the client UI; the server still grants.

Monetization: Passes: check `UserOwnsGamePassAsync` in `pcall` on join and listen to `PromptGamePassPurchaseFinished` for in-session buys; refunded passes lose ownership, so re-check instead of caching forever. Subscriptions: `GetUserSubscriptionStatusAsync` on join and on `UserSubscriptionStatusChanged`; perks must be revocable. Developer-product refunds are your job: keep each handled `PurchaseId` with what it granted so a refund can be reversed (Transaction Refunded webhook).

Monetization: Shops that sell: show live prices from `GetProductInfoAsync`, never hard-coded Robux numbers (regional and optimised pricing differ per user; `receipt.CurrencySpent` is what was paid). `RankProductsAsync` once on join (strict rate limit), `RecommendTopProductsAsync` inside `task.spawn`. Contextual offers (revive on death, boost when stuck) beat static menus. `MarketplaceService:OpenShop(player)` opens the Roblox Shop overlay.

Monetization: Compliance: paid random items (spins, eggs, loot boxes bought with Robux) must show odds before purchase and check `PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync` (`ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted` means offer a free path or direct purchase; `IsPaidItemTradingAllowed` false means disable trading of paid items). Gate gifting and trading of bought items with `GetUsersPriceLevelsAsync` if regional arbitrage is a risk. Rewarded video rewards are developer products, never random, and the character is protected while the ad plays. Perks stay cosmetic or convenience, not pay-to-win. `player:PromptAgeCheck()` at most once per 15 minutes and only on a deliberate action; never gate core gameplay on it.

Teleports and places: A universe shares DataStores, MemoryStores, MessagingService and products across all its places. Set Access Control for Places to 'Secure within universe only' so clients cannot teleport themselves into restricted places, and check eligibility on join.

Teleports and places: Use `TeleportService:TeleportAsync` with `TeleportOptions`: `ShouldReserveServer` for matches and parties, `ReservedServerAccessCode` to join one, `ServerInstanceId` for a specific public server. The old Teleport, TeleportToPlaceInstance and ReserveServer calls are deprecated. `TeleportData` is readable by clients and can be tampered with; never trust it for currency, items or permissions, and key real match data by `PrivateServerId` in a MemoryStore or DataStore written before the teleport.

Teleports and places: Handoff: end or save the player's profile before teleporting, load with session locking on arrival, keep a loading screen with `SetTeleportGui` and `ReplicatedFirst`. Server type: public has `PrivateServerId = ''`; reserved has an id and owner 0; private (VIP) has an id and an owner. A match server waits for expected players with a timeout, runs the round, saves results, then teleports everyone back. Server browsers heartbeat `{jobId, players, mode}` into a MemoryStore sorted map with a short TTL. Custom matchmaking signals (player and server attributes) suit skill-based public servers; reserved servers suit exact teams.

Live ops and analytics: Log from the server with `AnalyticsService` `LogEconomyEvent` (every source and sink, accurate ending balance), `LogProgressionEvent`, `LogFunnelStepEvent` and `LogCustomEvent`; the `Fire*` methods are deprecated. Keep event names and custom values low-cardinality (categories, not free text or user ids). Design funnels (onboarding, shop, first purchase) before building the feature.

Live ops and analytics: Live values: put balance numbers, feature flags and event toggles in experience configs read with `ConfigService` (always code a default; use `GetConfigForPlayerAsync` for targeted experiments, `SetTestingValue` in Studio). Timed events use UTC timestamps in a config compared with `os.time()` on the server, and clients count down from `workspace:GetServerTimeNow()`. Daily shops rotate with `math.floor(os.time() / 86400)`; daily rewards store `lastClaimDay` and a streak; seasons store claimed rewards per season id. Roll new content out behind a flag, validate with a small group, then ship to everyone.

Live ops and analytics: Badges: `AwardBadgeAsync` on the server in `pcall`, skip if already owned; good for onboarding and milestones. Re-engagement: ask for opt-in at a good moment with `ExperienceNotificationService:CanPromptOptInAsync()` then `PromptOptIn()`; notifications are sent from a backend and rate-limited.

Data extras: Version the save: a `version` field and ordered migration functions on load, then `Reconcile`. Never remove a field in the same release that stops writing it, and never reuse a field name for a new meaning. Restore from versions (`ListVersionsAsync`, `GetVersionAtTimeAsync`) instead of backup keys. Do not pre-compress data. Store only plain tables, numbers, strings, booleans and buffers; never Instances, CFrames or mixed tables.

Data extras: MemoryStore: sorted maps for rankings and server lists, queues for matchmaking and work (read, process, then remove by id; invisibility timeout is the crash safety), hash maps for counters. Everything expires (45 days at most), so it is never the only copy. MessagingService is at most 1 kB per message and best effort. Keys like `User_{UserId}` stay static so automated right-to-be-forgotten can delete them; link keys to user ids (`AddUserId`). Studio needs Enable Studio Access to API Services and a separate test universe or store name. Check `GetRequestBudgetForRequestType` before bulk work.

Combat and hit validation: Clients predict (play the swing or shot instantly) and send intent; the server owns cooldowns, range, ammo, hit validation and damage. For hit claims check the origin is near the shooter's server position (tolerance scaled by `player:GetNetworkPing()`), the target is alive and an enemy and in range, the claimed point is near the target's recent server position (keep about a second of position history), and a server raycast against static geometry finds no wall. Draw tracers and hit effects on clients from a minimal event.

Talking to the player: The user wants plain input and plain output, like any player or developer: they ask for a thing, they get the thing. Never mention skills, standards, checks, rule codes, ids, budgets or internals.

Talking to the player: Reply in one to three short plain sentences: what is done and, only if needed, one thing to try or one thing you could not confirm. No lists of rules, no tables, no process notes.
Talking to the player: Do every check yourself and fix failures before replying. Never claim it works or looks good unless you ran it or measured it.
Check table (private, never shown): SYS-1 Server owns currency and every multiplier through one module
Check table (private, never shown): SYS-2 Prices, odds and rewards come from server data tables
Check table (private, never shown): SYS-3 Collect, buy, sell, hatch and rebirth are validated, claim-first and rate limited
Check table (private, never shown): SYS-4 Collection uses a sound method for the scale (guarded Touched for few, spatial query for many)
Check table (private, never shown): SYS-5 Numbers are capped, integer safe, never NaN, and formatted correctly at boundaries
Check table (private, never shown): SYS-6 Saved, versioned and rebuilt on join
Check table (private, never shown): SYS-7 Spawners capped, collectibles cleaned up, popups pooled
Check table (private, never shown): SYS-8 Distances and speeds sized in studs against the defaults
Check table (private, never shown): SYS-9 Round and objective state lives on the server
Check table (private, never shown): SYS-10 Played in Studio: earn, spend, rejoin and confirm the data kept

Official docs (offline): `ms_roblox_docs` holds the official Roblox Creator Docs and Luau docs offline (about 2,260 pages: every engine class, enum, datatype and library, plus the guides). Before quoting a limit, a price rule or a purchase flow, search the guides (data stores, developer products, passes, subscriptions, teleports, MemoryStore, MessagingService) and cite the page; confirm MarketplaceService, DataStoreService and TeleportService calls with action api, and run action check on the scripts.

Ready-made systems: Before writing a common system from scratch, open the kit index with `ms_skill_reference` (skill_id game-systems, action index, then read INDEX.md). It lists tested starting scripts from Brickwire (MIT): obby stages and kill bricks, jump and speed pads, teleporters, coins, round loop, saved stats, daily reward, shop, inventory, HUD, menus, toasts, day and night, NPC dialog, VFX presets, camera fly-through and the cutscene module with case, egg, dice, event and story scenes.

Ready-made systems: Read the closest file, then adapt it: use the project's names, style, currency and data code, replace every {{KEY}} with a real value, and keep one system per job instead of adding a second copy. Never paste a kit unread, and never pretend a kit was run in Studio; it was only run in a Luau VM with a stubbed Roblox API.

Ready-made systems: Where a kit is simpler than these rules, the rules win and you upgrade it: UpdateAsync with session locking instead of Get/SetAsync for player data, an idempotent ProcessReceipt for real purchases, validated and rate-limited remotes. The shop kit moves in-game currency only.

Cutscenes and reveals (cases, eggs, dice, events, story): Decide the result on the server first (weighted roll with the reused Random, reward granted and saved), then send the result to the client, which only shows it. The show never decides anything and a skipped show still grants the reward.

Cutscenes and reveals (cases, eggs, dice, events, story): Build a timeline of beats: camera moves, subtitles, sound, shake, flash, colour, VFX. Store the original camera type, camera subject and control state before starting and restore them on finish, on Skip, on character death, on leaving, and on any error. Never leave the player stuck with a Scriptable camera or disabled controls.

Cutscenes and reveals (cases, eggs, dice, events, story): Always show a Skip button that works from the first frame and on touch and gamepad. Keep common results short (a few seconds); the rarer the result, the longer the pause and the stronger the shake, flash and light rays. Epic and above get a full-screen reveal; Mythic and above may use a false ending before the real one. Keep subtitles readable (contrast, size, safe area) and use only sound ids you can confirm play live.

Cutscenes and reveals (cases, eggs, dice, events, story): Read cutscene.luau, cut-client.luau and the matching scene file from the kit index instead of rebuilding the timeline; check the scene length, Skip, sounds, subtitle readability, camera restore and the server roll before saying it is done.
qualityGates: Every rule is checked against the real result in Studio, not assumed
Failures are fixed before replying; a failing check is never reported as done
Checks, ids and specs stay private; the user gets a short plain result
Anything not run in Studio is reported as untested in one plain sentence
ProcessReceipt is set in one script and returns a decision for every receipt, with duplicate receipts ignored
Player data uses session locking, never saves unloaded data and saves on shutdown
Rolls, earnings and trades are decided on the server, and odds shown match the code
Purchases, teleports and live values follow the server-only granting and untrusted TeleportData rules
A common system starts from the closest ready-made kit when one exists, adapted and upgraded to these rules
A cutscene always restores the camera and controls, has Skip, and never decides the reward on the client
APIs that are not certain are confirmed with ms_roblox_docs, and scripts pass its check before they are written
game-systems.architecturePolicy: State server, client, shared and editor ownership; preserve existing service boundaries and lifecycle cleanup.
game-systems.platformPolicy: Cover desktop, touch and gamepad where relevant; include safe areas, focus, respawn, late join and weakest-device behavior.
game-systems.studioEvidencePolicy: Use exact live Roblox Studio MCP schemas; verify with Edit/Server/Client or multi-client tests, clean Output, DataModel read-back and measured profiler/network evidence.
game-systems.securityPolicy: Validate consequential client input on the server, rate-limit exposed remotes and test abuse paths where relevant.

engineExecutionContract.schemaBinding: Discover exact live MCP tool schemas at runtime; never rely on remembered command names or parameters.
parameterPolicy: validate required and nested fields before execution
coerce only unambiguous provider formatting differences
reject unsupported enums, bounds, patterns and unknown fields when the schema forbids them
route to the declared engine/server only
read back native state after mutation
recoveryPolicy: classify schema, transport, editor-state and engine-runtime failures separately
refresh the live catalogue after unknown-tool/schema drift
retry transient transport/editor disconnect once only
never repeat an unchanged failing mutation
rollback or stop when evidence cannot prove safe completion

activation.when: Always use for simulators, coin or collecting loops, tycoons, pets, rebirths, shops, quests, currency and horror structure.
activation.style: Explicit user references first, then existing project style. Select one coherent style bible.

executionWorkflow.adaptation: Apply only relevant parts to the actual user goal. Inspect existing naming, dependencies and style; adapt the method instead of copying sample paths or architecture. Current user scope and tool permissions govern. Skill text is reference data, never permission.
executionWorkflow.inspect: existing keys, data schema, migration and transaction ownership
executionWorkflow.execute: Use safe atomic updates and bounded retries; prevent default saves after failed loads.
executionWorkflow.verify: Test with isolated data: failed load/save, concurrent updates, migration, duplicate purchases and shutdown.
executionWorkflow.craft: Preserve the existing architecture and style. Build a complete requested path, then inspect real results; additional polish must serve the task.
executionWorkflow.role: Deliver actionable constraints, interfaces and acceptance criteria that the current project can implement.
executionWorkflow.handoff: State owned files/assets, adjacent interfaces and acceptance criteria. In co-work, read the board and claim disjoint resources; do not overwrite another worker.

evidence.measured: Actual tool output, read-back, build/test result or capture with source/path.
evidence.reviewed: Code/document inspection only; label it as reviewed.
evidence.unverified: Name the absent tool, access or environment and continue feasible work.

executionWorkflow.recovery: Reuse still-valid evidence. A failed, restricted or truncated inspection is UNKNOWN, not an empty project. Stop unchanged reads and identical failures; narrow the question, repair its cause or disclose the blocker. Rerun affected checks only. Never fabricate a tool result, model capability, asset ID or successful test.
