scripting-power.description: Always use for powerful Roblox scripting: official Luau speed rules, types, task and cleanup patterns, remote and data safety, Parallel Luau, physics queries, profiling, and the best community tools.
scripting-power.whenToUse: Always use when making Roblox code fast, safe or easy to change: performance and lag, memory, types, async and cleanup, remotes and security, saving data, parallel work, physics queries, tooling, or architecture.
steps: Mandatory standard for writing powerful Roblox code. Built from the official Roblox and Luau docs plus the best community tools. The rules below are the tricks, limits and traps that decide whether code is fast, safe and easy to change. Use the ones the task touches.

Core: Write modern Luau: `continue`, compound assignment (`+=`, `..=`), if-expressions (`if x then a else b`), backtick string interpolation (`Hello {name}`), generalized iteration (`for k, v in t do`), `//` floor division, and `--!strict` at the top of scripts. Do not write old Lua 5.1 habits when Luau has a better form.
Core: Never trust `a and b or c` when `b` can be false or nil: use `if a then b else c`. Never write `not x == y` (it parses as `(not x) == y`).

Core: Use the task library, not the old globals: `task.wait`, `task.spawn`, `task.defer`, `task.delay`, `task.cancel`. The globals `wait`, `spawn` and `delay` are marked Deprecated in the official reference.
Core: Prefer `obj:Method()` over `obj.Method(obj)`, constant field names (`t.field`), and tables with the same shape every time. Keep object tables uniform; varying keys slows field access.
Core: Never use `getfenv`, `setfenv` or `loadstring` in game code. They switch off compiler optimisations (even a read of getfenv does), and loadstring is also a security risk.

Core: Pre-size big arrays with `table.create(n, value)`. Use `table.insert` to append when the size is unknown. Use `table.clear(t)` to empty a table you will reuse (it keeps its capacity), and `table.find` instead of a hand-written search loop.
Core: Avoid creating tables, closures or Instances inside hot loops and per-frame callbacks. Reuse them, or build them once outside. Per-frame code must stay tiny.

Core: Cache lookups you use many times: hold the result of `FindFirstChild`, `GetService` or a deep path in a local once instead of searching each frame. A community benchmark measured FindFirstChild about 8x slower than a stored reference.
Core: Set every property before parenting, and set `.Parent` last, instead of `Instance.new("Part", parent)`. Parenting first makes each later change replicate separately.
Core: Check results before indexing. `FindFirstChild`, `GetAttribute`, `Raycast`, `GetNetworkOwner` and `Clone` (when Archivable is false) can all return nil.

Core: Add `@native` above a hot, numeric function (or `--!native` for a whole script) and annotate parameters (especially `Vector3`). Only do this for heavy math run often; it is wasted on code that mostly calls Roblox APIs.

Core: Return a single module table, keep requires at the top, and never yield forever or require recursively. A ModuleScript runs once and is cached, so state in it is shared by every script that requires it.

Luau speed: Fastcall built-ins are called directly (`math.max(x, 1)`) or through a local alias. `string.byte(s)` beats `s:byte()`. `math.random`, `math.randomseed` and `math.noise` are not fastcalls. Math fastcalls take numbers only; strings go through a slower path.

Luau speed: Table literals with all fields at once are the fastest way to build an object. For a sequential fill of a pre-sized array, explicit index assignment is fastest. `#t` is cheap because the length is cached.

Luau speed: The fastest object layout is a table whose metatable's `__index` points to a table (ideally itself). Avoid `__index` functions and long inheritance chains in hot code. Static fields should be read as `Class.Field`, not `object.Field`.

Luau speed: Upvalues that are never reassigned are captured by value with no allocation; reassigned ones need an extra object. Closures with no upvalues, or only immutable module-level ones, are cached. Function identity can therefore be shared, which matters if you use functions as table keys.

Luau speed: Native `vector` values (Vector3 in Luau-native form) avoid garbage. Constant loops like `for i = 1, 4` are unrolled and small local functions are inlined by the compiler (not when getfenv or setfenv is used).
Luau speed: Generalized iteration (`for k, v in t do`) is as fast as pairs/ipairs and skips the call. `for i = 1, #t` is slightly slower. `select(n, ...)` is cheap under fastcall.
Luau speed: Remove `print` and `warn` from hot paths in shipped builds. Debug output costs time and floods the log.

Native and profiling: `--!native` at the top applies to the whole script, `@native` to one function. Behaviour never changes, only speed. Gains come from numeric code, math on tables or buffers, functions called often, and typed arguments such as `v: Vector3`.

Native and profiling: Native does not help top-level code that runs once, code heavy on Roblox API or library calls, built-ins called with non-number arguments, or arguments that do not match their annotations. It adds startup time and memory, so do not put it on every script. Breakpoints in a function turn its native version off.

Native and profiling: Native limits: 64K instructions per block, 1 million per script, and a total native memory cap after which code runs non-native. Check it worked: the Script Profiler shows `<native>`, and `debug.dumpcodesize()` (Server view, Command Bar) reports native size.

Native and profiling: Measure before and after with `os.clock()` around a loop of many runs, or wrap code in `debug.profilebegin("Name")` and `debug.profileend()` to get a named label in the MicroProfiler. Never optimise by feel.

Native and profiling: MicroProfiler opens with Ctrl+F6 (Cmd+F6) in Studio or the client. Pause a spike with Ctrl+P, find wide labels, and add profile scopes to narrow it down. Orange frames mean worker threads (scripts, physics, animation); blue means the render thread; red means render time over job time with GPU wait above 2.5 ms.
Native and profiling: For the server use the Developer Console (Ctrl+F9) Server tab, which captures up to 60 frames. Frame budgets: 16.67 ms for 60 FPS, 33.33 ms for 30 FPS, 8.33 ms for 120 FPS.

Language features: `const` bindings cannot be reassigned (the table they hold can still change). Attributes are written `@name` before a function (the supported one for games is `@native`). Number literals allow `0b0101`, `0xFF` and `1_000_000`.
Language features: `continue` must be the last statement in its block. Compound assignments are statements, not expressions. If-then-else expressions need an `else`.

Language features: Strings allow `\u{1F600}` and `\xAB` escapes and `\z` to skip whitespace. Integer literals above 2^53 lose precision and trigger a warning; add `.0` to silence it only if that is truly intended.

Types: `--!nocheck` turns checking off, `--!nonstrict` checks only annotated variables (the rest are `any`), `--!strict` infers and checks everything. Put the comment on the first line. Prefer `--!strict` for new modules.

Types: Syntax: `local n: number`, optional `string?`, union `A | B`, intersection `A & B`, generics `type List<T> = {T}`, `type Map<K, V> = {[K]: V}`, `typeof(value)`, cast `v :: any`, `export type Cat = {Name: string}` (types do not cross ModuleScripts unless exported), literal types like `"hi"`.

Types: Gotchas: Luau has no `table` type (write `{number}`, `{[string]: number}` or `{Speed: number}`). A function type's variadics are `(...number) -> number`, but a function declaration's are `(...: number)`. Multiple returns need parentheses: `(string, number)`. `?` still allows nil, so check. `::` is not a conversion; only `:: any` bypasses a mismatch.

Types: Annotate public function parameters and returns, module tables and data records. Type your own classes with an `export type` and a `.new` constructor that returns it. Typed code also feeds native compilation.

Library tricks: `table.clone(t)` makes a shallow copy (nested tables are still shared, deep copy with a recursive function). `table.freeze(t)` makes a table read-only for good (shallow; there is no unfreeze). Freeze config and constants so a typo cannot change them.

Library tricks: `math.clamp`, `math.lerp(a, b, t)`, `math.map(x, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax)`, `math.sign`, `math.round`, `math.isfinite`/`isnan`/`isinf`. `math.clamp` errors if min is greater than max.

Library tricks: `string.split(s, sep)`, `string.pack`/`unpack` for binary, `utf8.len(s)` (returns nil plus the bad byte position for invalid text). Use `utf8` for player text, never `#` for character counts.

Library tricks: `buffer` is fixed-size mutable memory: `buffer.create(n)`, `buffer.readi32/writei32`, `readf32`, `readu8`, `buffer.readbits/writebits`, `buffer.copy`, `buffer.fill`, `buffer.tostring/fromstring`. Use buffers to pack network data and to hold big numeric grids with no per-element garbage. Reads and writes are little-endian.

Library tricks: `bit32.band/bor/bxor/extract/replace/countlz` for flags and packed fields. `vector.create`, `vector.dot`, `vector.cross`, `vector.normalize`, `vector.magnitude` for native-vector math. `coroutine.close(co)` ends a suspended coroutine.
Library tricks: Use `os.clock()` for timing short work, `os.time()` for a timestamp, `workspace:GetServerTimeNow()` when all players must agree on a time.

Async and cleanup: `task.spawn` runs the function now; `task.defer` runs it at the end of the current resumption cycle; `task.delay(t, fn)` runs it later. All return a thread you can pass to `task.cancel`. Store the thread if you may need to stop it.

Async and cleanup: Code that yields (`WaitForChild`, `:Wait()`, DataStore calls, `InvokeServer`, `task.wait`) must never block a place that must stay responsive: wrap it in `task.spawn`, or return a Promise. An error inside a spawned thread only kills that thread; it does not stop the script.

Async and cleanup: Every `:Connect` needs an owner. Keep connections in a table or use a cleanup helper (Trove or Janitor from RbxUtil/Janitor, or a Maid) and disconnect or destroy it when the owner goes away. Destroying an Instance disconnects its own events, but connections to outside objects (for example RunService or a Players signal) stay alive until you disconnect them.

Async and cleanup: For per-player systems, create the state on join and clear it in `PlayerRemoving`. Clear cooldown tables, rate-limit tables and connection tables there too, or the server grows forever.

Async and cleanup: Debounce and cooldowns: store `os.clock()` per player (or per object) and compare, instead of `task.wait` loops. `Touched` fires many times per contact, so always debounce anything that costs.

Async and cleanup: Promises (evaera's roblox-lua-promise) turn yield-based code into composable values with `andThen`, `catch`, `finally`, `Promise.all`, `race`, `retry`, `delay`. Use them when several async steps must be chained, retried or cancelled, and use plain `task.spawn` for fire-and-forget.
Async and cleanup: Signal (RbxUtil) is a custom event class. Use it for module-to-module events inside your own code instead of BindableEvents; it passes tables by reference and has no copy cost.

Async and cleanup: Pool things you create and destroy often (bullets, damage numbers, effects): keep a stack of parked instances, move them far away or set transparency, and reuse them rather than `Clone` and `Destroy` every time. `Debris:AddItem(obj, seconds)` is fine for rare one-off cleanup (it defaults to 10 seconds).

Networking: RemoteEvent is one-way and does not yield; RemoteFunction yields the caller. The server handler's first argument is always the Player. Clients cannot talk to each other; relay through the server.

Networking: What survives a remote: numbers, strings, booleans, Enums and replicable Instances. Functions arrive as nil. Instances the receiver cannot see (such as ServerStorage children) arrive as nil. Non-string table keys become strings, mixed array/dictionary tables and nil holes lose data, metatables are lost, and tables are copies.
Networking: Never use `InvokeClient`. A client that errors, leaves, or returns nothing makes the server throw or yield forever. Use a RemoteEvent in each direction for replies.

Networking: Order: RemoteEvents are reliable and ordered, across different RemoteEvents. RemoteFunctions are not ordered against RemoteEvents, so use one kind or add a sequence number. UnreliableRemoteEvent can drop or reorder messages (and payloads over 1,000 bytes), so use it for frequent, non-critical updates like cosmetic positions, with a timestamp or sequence number to ignore stale data.

Networking: Bandwidth: fewer, larger remote calls beat many small ones. Pack data into buffers (a typed library like Zap generates this from a schema, packs tightly, and validates incoming data). Drive purely visual effects on each client from one small signal rather than replicating the effect's parts. A community guide suggests keeping network use around 80 KB/s per client as a rough goal.

Networking: Create remotes once at startup in ReplicatedStorage, name them clearly, and connect the server handler before any client can fire. Client-to-server rate limits are shared per remote type; excess reliable calls are delayed and excess unreliable ones are dropped.

Networking: BindableEvent: Fire does not yield, each listener runs in its own thread in an unpredictable order, and tables are copied (metatables lost). BindableFunction: Invoke yields, only one OnInvoke callback exists, and a missing return gives nil.

Security: The client is never trusted. On every remote the server must check the type of each argument, reject NaN and infinity with `math.isfinite`, check numbers are in a sane range (positive quantities, valid ids), cap string length, and for an Instance argument check it is the right class and in the right place.

Security: The server must also check context: is the player alive, close enough, holding the item, off cooldown, allowed to do this now. Re-check hit claims against server state (an origin that is allowed to be a little late is fine, an impossible one is not).

Security: Rate-limit everything a client can trigger (remotes, Touched, ProximityPrompt, ClickDetector), on the server, with a token bucket for short bursts. Give more care to expensive actions: DataStore and BadgeService calls, teleports and currency grants. Clear the player's limiter on leave.

Security: Do not accept paths or instances to modify or delete, do not `require` or load assets from client arguments, and do not let the client set authoritative state. Properties like Enabled or MaxActivationDistance set on the client are not authoritative. Only the ProximityPrompt `Triggered` event is distance-checked by the server; ClickDetector events are not.

Security: Confirm purchases in `ProcessReceipt`, never from `PromptProductPurchaseFinished`. A part a client has network ownership of can be moved by that client, so keep unowned-critical parts anchored or server-owned, and keep important parts server-controlled with `SetNetworkOwner(nil)`.

Data: Data limits (official): name, key and scope 50 characters; value 4,194,304 characters; per key 4 MB write and 25 MB read per minute; each request rounds up to 1 KB; the queue holds 30 requests. Per server, standard read and write allow 60 + players x 40 requests per minute.

Data: Errors worth knowing: 105 value too large; 301 to 306 request dropped because the queue is full; 403 Studio API access off; 502 service rejected the request and 504 malformed response. `DatastoreThrottled`, `KeyThrottled` and `InternalServerError` need a retry with exponential backoff.

Data: Always wrap data calls in `pcall`, retry with exponential backoff, and when loading fails after the retries do not save a default over the player's real data: kick with a clear message and try again later. Never save before the load finished.

Data: Use session locking so two servers never write the same player at once (it prevents duplication). ProfileStore does this: `ProfileStore.New(name, template)`, `store:StartSessionAsync(key, {Cancel = fn})` (nil on failure), `profile:AddUserId`, `profile:Reconcile()` to fill new template keys, `profile.OnSessionEnd` (kick the player when another server takes the lock), `profile:EndSession()` on leave. Default autosave is 300 seconds.

Data: ProfileStore pattern: on PlayerAdded start the session with a Cancel that checks the player is still in the game; on success add the user id, reconcile, connect OnSessionEnd, store it in a table, and if the player already left end the session; on nil kick with a rejoin message; also run the same code for players already present; on PlayerRemoving end the session. It is for per-player data, not leaderboards or global state.

Data: Use `UpdateAsync` (not `SetAsync`) so concurrent writes cannot overwrite each other. Save in `game:BindToClose` once, at startup, for every player (do not bind it inside PlayerRemoving), and guard against saving the same player twice. Do not store Instances; cap string lengths; table keys must not be NaN or nil.

Data: `MarketplaceService.ProcessReceipt` can be set once, by one server script. Record the grant durably (for example in an UpdateAsync keyed by `receiptInfo.PurchaseId`), return `PurchaseGranted` only after it is saved, return `NotProcessedYet` if the player is gone or a save failed, make it idempotent so a redelivered receipt never grants twice, and never yield inside the UpdateAsync callback.

Data: `UserOwnsGamePassAsync` yields and can fail: wrap it in pcall and cache the result per player. MemoryStore (HashMap, SortedMap, Queue) is for short-lived shared state across servers like matchmaking or event queues; MessagingService is for server-to-server notices (`PublishAsync` and `SubscribeAsync`), and neither is a place to keep permanent data.

Parallel Luau: Scripts run serially unless they sit under an `Actor`. Each Actor can run on its own core; scripts in the same Actor stay sequential, so use several Actors for real parallelism. A script belongs to its closest Actor ancestor.

Parallel Luau: `task.desynchronize()` moves to parallel and `task.synchronize()` moves back. `RBXScriptSignal:ConnectParallel(fn)` runs the callback in parallel (do not call desynchronize inside it). You cannot `require` in a parallel phase; require first, serially. Compute in parallel, then synchronize to write to Instances.

Parallel Luau: Each API member has a thread-safety tag: Unsafe (default), Read Parallel, Local Safe, Safe. The engine blocks unsafe access. Check the tag in the reference before using a member in parallel. Raycast, Blockcast, Spherecast and the GetPartBounds functions are Write Parallel.

Parallel Luau: Talk between Actors with `Actor:SendMessage(topic, ...)`, `BindToMessage` (serial) or `BindToMessageParallel`, or share large data in a `SharedTable` (not copied, atomic, visible to all). Keep what you send small. Long unyielding work blocks even in parallel, so split it. Good for: pathfinding for many NPCs, procedural generation, heavy raycasts.

Physics and queries: `workspace:Raycast(origin, direction, params)` returns a result or nil; the direction vector's length is the distance. Use `RaycastParams` with `FilterDescendantsInstances` and `FilterType`, a `CollisionGroup`, `IgnoreWater`, and set `RespectCanCollide = true` if you want non-collidable parts ignored (it is false by default). `Spherecast`, `Blockcast` and `Shapecast` sweep shapes along a direction.

Physics and queries: `GetPartBoundsInBox`, `GetPartBoundsInRadius` and `GetPartsInPart` take `OverlapParams` (set `MaxParts`). Use them for area damage and triggers instead of many Touched connections. The old Region3 `FindParts*` functions are deprecated.

Physics and queries: Collision groups: `workspace:RegisterCollisionGroup(name)`, set `part.CollisionGroup`, then `workspace:CollisionGroupSetCollidable(a, b, false)` (check with `CollisionGroupsAreCollidable`). Use them to stop players colliding with each other, or NPCs with their own bullets.

Physics and queries: Network ownership: `part:SetNetworkOwner(player or nil)` (check `CanSetNetworkOwnership()` first). Unanchored parts near a player are usually owned by that client, so critical server-side physics (projectiles, pickups) should be `SetNetworkOwner(nil)` or anchored. A pure visual can be simulated on the client.

Physics and queries: Turn off what you do not need on parts that never move or never need it: `Anchored = true`, `CanCollide`, `CanTouch`, `CanQuery`, `CastShadow` (small parts). Use `CollisionFidelity` Box or Hull instead of Precise where you can. `Touched` needs at least one unanchored, moving part.

Physics and queries: Replace body movers (`BodyVelocity`, `BodyPosition`, `BodyGyro` and so on, all deprecated) with the physics constraints (`LinearVelocity`, `AlignPosition`, `AlignOrientation`, `VectorForce`).

Players and streaming: `Players.PlayerAdded` only fires for players who join after you connect, so also loop `Players:GetPlayers()` once at startup. `PlayerRemoving(player, reason)` fires while the player is still listed. `CharacterAdded` fires each respawn, so connect Humanoid events inside it, and also handle `player.Character` if it already exists.

Players and streaming: `CharacterAutoLoads = false` means you must call `player:LoadCharacterAsync()` yourself to respawn. `Humanoid.Died` needs connecting on every new character. Use `Humanoid:TakeDamage` for damage and change health on the server only.

Players and streaming: With StreamingEnabled, only Workspace descendants stream (ReplicatedStorage does not). On a client, an Atomic model streams in together, so `WaitForChild` the model itself; a Persistent model arrives before `Workspace.PersistentLoaded`; a streamed-out instance gets Parent = nil but is not destroyed. Write client code that tolerates parts appearing and disappearing, and do not rely on client-only property changes surviving a stream-out.

Players and streaming: Do not use `WaitForChild` on everything: it is for things that must arrive, with a timeout and a plan if it never does. Use `Persistent` models rarely and keep replication focus additions few.

Input and frame loop: `InputBegan(input, gameProcessed)`: ignore the input when `gameProcessed` is true (typing in a text box or clicking UI). Input code belongs in LocalScripts. Use `UserInputService.TouchEnabled`, `GamepadEnabled` and `PreferredInput` to adapt the UI, and support touch, gamepad and keyboard for every action.

Input and frame loop: `ContextActionService:BindAction(name, handler, createTouchButton, ...)` gives mobile buttons and clean rebinding. The handler gets (actionName, inputState, inputObject); return `Enum.ContextActionResult.Pass` to let other handlers also see the input; it sinks by default. Unbind with `UnbindAction` (for example on Unequipped).

Input and frame loop: `RunService.PreRender` (client, before drawing), `PreSimulation`, `PostSimulation` and `Heartbeat` each pass delta time. Use `BindToRenderStep(name, priority, fn)` for camera and visual work that must run each frame, and unbind it with `UnbindFromRenderStep`. Put visual-only effects at the Last priority. Always multiply motion by delta time, never assume a frame rate.

Input and frame loop: `TweenService:Create(obj, TweenInfo.new(time, style, direction, repeatCount, reverses, delay), {Prop = value})` does not start itself: call `:Play()`. Repeat count below zero loops forever. Use tweens for UI and simple motion instead of per-frame loops.

Input and frame loop: `CollectionService` tags are the clean way to give behaviour to many objects: `AddTag`, then connect `GetInstanceAddedSignal(tag)` AND loop `GetTagged(tag)` for ones that already exist (existing instances do not fire the added signal), and use `GetInstanceRemovedSignal(tag)` to clean up. Attributes (`SetAttribute`, `GetAttributeChangedSignal`) are the clean way to give each object its own settings.

Architecture and style: The server owns state and rules; the client owns presentation and input. One script per job; logic lives in ModuleScripts; scripts are thin glue. Keep server-only code in ServerScriptService and server-only assets in ServerStorage, not ReplicatedStorage.

Architecture and style: Roblox's Lua style guide: PascalCase for classes, enum-like tables and Roblox APIs; camelCase for locals, members and functions; LOUD_SNAKE_CASE for constants; a leading underscore for private members; file names match the exported object; no abbreviations.

Architecture and style: File order: purpose comment, services via `GetService`, requires (sorted, at the top), constants, module variables and functions, the returned object, `return`. Comment why, not what. Only use metatables for prototype-style classes and typo guards.

Architecture and style: Class pattern: `local Class = {}`, `Class.__index = Class`, `export type Class = typeof(setmetatable({} :: {field: T}, Class))`, `function Class.new(...): Class ... return setmetatable(self, Class) end`, methods defined with dot syntax and an explicit typed `self`, called with a colon. Use composition over deep inheritance.

Architecture and style: Functions that can fail should return `success, result` (or a Result or Promise), and only throw to flag misuse. Wrap calls that may throw in `pcall` with a comment of what error you expect. Do not hide errors with an empty pcall.

Architecture and style: For large games consider an ECS (Matter) when you have thousands of similar entities with data-driven systems, and a state library (Fusion or similar) for complex reactive UI. For small and medium games plain modules, attributes and tags are simpler; do not add a framework the game does not need.

Tooling: Rojo syncs files on disk to Studio so you can use real editors and Git. Pair it with Wally (package manager: `wally.toml` for the manifest, `wally.lock` for exact versions, `wally install`), luau-lsp (language server with Roblox types; generate a `sourcemap.json` with `rojo sourcemap --watch`), Selene (linter), StyLua (formatter), and Moonwave (docs).

Tooling: luau-lsp also has `luau-lsp analyze` for type and lint checks in CI. Configure strictness and lints in `.luaurc`. Add `sourcemap.json` to `.gitignore`. A companion Studio plugin supplies DataModel information for instances that are not in your Rojo build.

Tooling: Test pure logic with Jest Roblox (a port of Jest 27; test files named `*.spec.luau` in `__tests__`, `describe`, `it`, `expect`). It can run in Studio or in CI through Open Cloud Luau Execution. Keep game logic in pure ModuleScripts so it can be tested without a running game.

Tooling: RbxUtil has useful modules: Signal, Trove, Comm, Timer, TableUtil, Input, BufferUtil, Component, Concur, Spring, Shake, TaskQueue, TypedRemote, WaitFor. roblox-ts compiles TypeScript to Luau: good for big typed codebases, but debugging shows compiled Luau.

Lint-catchable bugs: Run Studio's script analysis and read these warnings seriously: UnknownGlobal (typos), ForRange (loops that run once or never), ImplicitReturn (function sometimes returns a value), DuplicateLocal, FormatString, TableLiteral (duplicate keys), UninitializedLocal, DuplicateFunction, DeprecatedApi, TableOperations (`#` or `ipairs` on a dictionary), DuplicateCondition, MisleadingAndOr, ComparisonPrecedence, UnreachableCode, BuiltinGlobalWrite, LocalShadow, and unused locals or imports.

Debugging: Read the first error in Output, not the last, and the line number. Use breakpoints, conditional breakpoints and the Watch window instead of print spam. Test in a real Server and Client window (Test tab), because many bugs only show on one side. Check the Developer Console (F9) for the live server.

Debugging: Memory leaks: watch memory grow over a long session in the Developer Console and the Luau heap; common causes are connections never disconnected, tables keyed by Instances or players that are never cleared, and instances held in caches. Weak tables (`__mode`) can hold caches without keeping objects alive.

Optimization checklist: Measure first, then fix the biggest cost. Typical wins: fewer per-frame loops, event-driven code instead of polling, spatial queries instead of looping every object, pooling, fewer parts and particles, and fewer, larger remote calls.

Optimization checklist: Draw calls: parts, meshes and unions batch when they share type, material and texture; shadows, particles and UI do not batch. Use only transparency 0 or 1 where you can to avoid overdraw, prefer built-in materials, use one light rather than several overlapping, shrink oversized textures and audio.

Optimization checklist: NPCs: path-finding for 100+ NPCs will lag. Only simulate NPCs near players, disable unused Humanoid states with `SetStateEnabled`, use an AnimationController for static NPCs, and spawn them when players are near. Keep ReplicatedStorage lean.

Optimization checklist: Join time and memory matter most on mobile: lazy-load heavy assets, stream the world, and avoid duplicate imports of the same mesh or texture. Treat a 20 second load cut as worth the work and a 0.5 second one as probably not.
Verify: Run the code in Studio (Play) when you can, and check Output for errors and warnings. Anything you did not run is reported as untested in one sentence.

Security extras: Exploiters control their client: they run any Luau, fire any remote with any arguments at any rate, change local properties (WalkSpeed, prompt `Enabled`, `MaxActivationDistance`) and move anything they own. Clients send intent, never results. Validate every handler argument (type, structure, range, `math.isfinite`, string length, `IsA` and `IsDescendantOf` for instances), validate context (alive, in range, cooldown, owns the item) and rate limit with a token bucket. Look up prices and stats in server tables by id; never read them from client data. Prefer silent mitigation (clamp, drop, rubber-band) and escalate on repeated signals; delay visible consequences.

Security extras: ProximityPrompt and ClickDetector events can be fired from anywhere even when disabled (only `Triggered` gets a distance check), so re-check enabled state, distance, alive and cooldown on the server. `Touched` on client-owned parts can be faked or suppressed. Unanchored parts a client can own can be pulled to the exploiter: anchor them or `SetNetworkOwner(nil)`. Any replicating script or module can be decompiled and any replicated content data-mined, so keep server logic out of shared modules and unreleased content out of production places. Keys live in the Secrets store (`HttpService:GetSecret`). Movement checks compare XZ displacement per interval to max speed plus latency tolerance and exempt your own teleports. Use `Players.BanningEnabled` and time-limited bans.

Networking choices: Channels: `RemoteEvent` (reliable, ordered) is the default; `UnreliableRemoteEvent` (may drop or reorder; payload at most 1000 bytes, larger is dropped) for aim direction and cosmetic VFX; `RemoteFunction` only client to server; never `InvokeClient` (it yields forever if the client errors or leaves); attributes for state clients read. Define remotes once on the server from a central table so names cannot typo, and have clients `WaitForChild`.

Networking choices: What survives the wire: tables are copied (identity and metatables lost, functions become nil); do not mix array and dictionary keys or leave nil holes; non-string keys are converted to strings, so send arrays of pairs; instances arrive nil if the receiver cannot see them (ServerStorage, not streamed in yet). Server to client ordering versus property replication is not guaranteed. Send changes not full state, throttle input sends (about 20 Hz), send ids and enums as small numbers, batch small messages once per frame, send an end timestamp instead of countdown ticks (`workspace:GetServerTimeNow()`), and tween on clients. Profile with the MicroProfiler (`ProcessPackets`) and the Developer Console Network tab; reach for Zap or Blink generators when network cost shows in profiling.

Physics, input and characters: Use spatial queries, not `Touched`, for hit detection and zones; reuse `RaycastParams` and `OverlapParams` (`AddToFilter`), `RespectCanCollide`, `CollisionGroup`. Impact effects and damage by impact speed use `BasePart:BindToCollisionSummaries` (fires only where the part is simulated; send what others need through a validated remote). Collision groups are registered once at server start (max 32). Mover constraints need an Attachment and a realistic `MaxForce` (not `math.huge` unless intended) or parts fling. Jitter comes from conflicting ownership, constraints fighting, mass ratios beyond 1:100, or setting CFrame on unanchored parts every frame. `SetNetworkOwner(nil)` for server-run assemblies, a driver for vehicles; ownership flips cause hitches. Competitive games can use Workspace `AuthorityMode = Server` (server simulation with client prediction and rollback).

Physics, input and characters: Input: new gameplay controls use the Input Action System (`InputContext`, `InputAction`, `InputBinding`; contexts switch control schemes, `Priority` and `Sink` stop double-firing); every action needs keyboard, gamepad and touch bindings; always honour `gameProcessedEvent`; branch on `PreferredInput`, not `TouchEnabled`; no hover-only interactions; gamepad dead zone about 0.15. Cameras update in `BindToRenderStep` and smooth with `1 - math.exp(-speed * dt)`. Reserved keys (Esc, F9, F11, chat) cannot be overridden.

Physics, input and characters: Characters: custom spawns use `CharacterAutoLoads = false` and `LoadCharacterAsync` after data loads; rebuild per-character state on `CharacterAdded`. Play the local player's animations on the client and NPC animations on the server; load each `Animation` once per Animator and reuse the track; animation assets must be owned by or shared with the experience owner or they silently fail; use `IKControl` for look-at and foot planting. Tweens only on anchored parts or UI and on clients, never on the server per frame. `Tool.Activated` comes from the client, so validate rate and state on the server.

Open Cloud and HttpService: Use Open Cloud with an API key (minimum scopes, IP allowlist, expiry) from tools and servers, never legacy cookie web APIs and never keys in game scripts. Handle pagination (`nextPageToken`), long-running operations (poll until `done`), and 429 with exponential backoff and jitter (retry only 429 and 5xx). DataStore budgets are shared with live servers, so throttle bulk scripts. In games: Allow HTTP Requests on, server only, about 500 requests per minute per server for external URLs, always `pcall` and check `response.Success`, keys in the Secrets store. Prefer native APIs (`Players:BanAsync`, `DataStoreService`) over calling Open Cloud for the same thing. Webhooks cover refunds, subscriptions and erasure requests.

Testing and tooling: Keep rules in pure ModuleScripts (inputs to outputs, no services or yields) and pass dependencies in, so they test without Roblox. Jest Lua is the test framework (TestEZ is legacy). Playtest with Clients and Servers (2 or more players) because most multiplayer bugs only show then; use the Device Simulator and Network Simulator for phones and bad networks. Before shipping check late joiners and respawns, leaving mid-action, rejoin and save, spammed or malformed remotes, mobile, gamepad and keyboard, and no Output errors.

Testing and tooling: Toolchain when a repo uses it: Rojo (file system is the source of truth; `*.server.luau`, `*.client.luau`, `init.luau` mapping), Wally or pesde packages, Rokit to pin tools, luau-lsp for types, StyLua to format, selene to lint, Lune for scripts outside Roblox, roblox-ts if `tsconfig.json` is present (do not hand-edit generated Luau). Do not edit Rojo-synced scripts through Studio tools; they are overwritten.

Testing and tooling: Studio tool loop: list studios, read every script you will touch, edit with exact minimal changes, create instances with a script in Edit context wrapped in `ChangeHistoryService` recording so the user can undo it as one step, playtest, read the console, assert state with scripts in Server and Client contexts, capture the screen, stop play when done. Changes made during play are discarded. Inspect scripts inside inserted Creator Store models before keeping them (backdoors are common in free models). Do not claim success without evidence.

Talking to the player: do every check yourself and never mention skills, standards, checks, rule codes, libraries or internals unless the player asks. Reply in one to three short plain sentences about the result.

Every remote validates its arguments on the server
Data calls use pcall, retries and session locking, and never save before loading
Every connection has an owner that cleans it up
Anything not run in Studio is reported as untested in one sentence

blender-texture-baking.name: Blender Texture Baking
blender-texture-baking.description: Bake game textures with verified projection and target-material readback.
blender-texture-baking.whenToUse: Bake game textures with verified projection and target-material readback.
steps: Inspect the high/low objects, UV layers, material slots, transforms and target renderer. Duplicate or save before changing source geometry; choose the requested map types and a measured texture-size budget.

Set a non-overlapping destination UV layout and intended texel density. Identify the exact active bake image for every receiving material; do not bake into a random selected image or overwrite a shared production texture.

Confirm the installed Blender bake API and engine. For selected-to-active projection, verify which object is active, the selected sources, normals and cage/ray distances using a low-resolution diagnostic bake.
Choose tangent/object normal space and the target channel convention deliberately. Treat normal, roughness and mask maps as data; keep base-color processing consistent with the target material.
Bake a small isolated region first. Inspect missing projections, opposite-side hits, seams, padding and UV bleed; repair cage or topology causes instead of raising samples to conceal errors.
Produce final maps to explicit project paths, save the images and editable blend source, and record map role, dimensions, channel packing and destination material.
Reimport into the real target shader and inspect at gameplay distance under representative lighting. Test mip seams, orientation, compression and memory against the agreed budget.
If baking or target import is unavailable, retain the editable setup and name the missing step. Never call a saved image a successful target-engine material without readback.

blender-shape-keys.name: Blender Shape Keys
blender-shape-keys.description: Author topology-safe expression and corrective shape keys and verify their delivery.
blender-shape-keys.whenToUse: Author topology-safe expression and corrective shape keys and verify their delivery.
steps: Inspect the Basis, existing key blocks, topology, vertex correspondence, modifiers, drivers and armature. Preserve the original mesh and establish the intended expression or correction range.
Keep vertex count and order stable for the key workflow. Do not run remeshing, destructive retopology or an unrelated topology-changing modifier on the production keyed mesh.
Create or edit the named key relative to its intended reference. Work in isolated face/body regions and preserve volume at silhouettes and joints rather than moving the whole object.
Test the key at zero, its useful intermediate values and the intended extremes. Check eyes, lips, teeth, intersections and asymmetric regions in the actual camera and rig pose.
Combine the expression with the relevant armature poses and other keys. Add a corrective or revise the sculpt where additive combinations collapse volume or break contact.
Inspect driver dependencies and key ownership before wiring controls; use the existing rig conventions, avoid cyclic dependencies and preserve animator overrides.
Confirm that the target format and runtime support the required morph animation. Export a small test, reopen it and compare shape names, ranges, timing and deformation.
Preserve the editable rig and report any unsupported driver or morph transfer as a boundary. A screenshot of one expression does not verify blended facial motion.

blender-geometry-nodes.name: Blender Geometry Nodes
blender-geometry-nodes.description: Build editable procedural node systems with bounded evaluation and verified exported geometry.
blender-geometry-nodes.whenToUse: Build editable procedural node systems with bounded evaluation and verified exported geometry.
steps: Inspect the current node groups, exposed sockets, object scale, instance sources, named attributes and target export requirements. Keep a reversible source group and define the smallest requested procedural variation.
Expose meaningful controls with units, useful defaults and sensible limits. Separate distribution, shape generation, material assignment and output; preserve stable names used by callers.
Prefer instances for repeated source geometry and measure instance/face counts. Realizing instances creates independent geometry and can sharply increase memory and evaluation cost.
Use deterministic seeds for reproducible comparisons and inspect attribute domains where a field is evaluated. Test minimum, typical and maximum settings rather than only the attractive default.
Realize only the necessary branch when a downstream operation or exporter needs real geometry. Check that attributes, material indices, normals and transforms survive that boundary.
Inspect evaluated bounds, density, overlaps, collision needs and renderer cost. Reduce the actual dominant workload before adding detail or random variation.
Export a controlled copy without destroying the procedural authoring source, then reimport to verify object scale, materials and topology in the target renderer or engine.
If a node/socket differs in the installed version, inspect the real API and repair that specific link. Do not silently substitute unrelated geometry or claim an untested export.

blender-sculpt-retopology.name: Blender Sculpt Retopology
blender-sculpt-retopology.description: Retopologize sculpted source into deformation-aware game meshes without destroying the sculpt.
blender-sculpt-retopology.whenToUse: Retopologize sculpted source into deformation-aware game meshes without destroying the sculpt.
steps: Preserve the high-resolution sculpt and inspect silhouette, symmetry, articulation, camera distance and target triangle budget. Choose a retopology method from the asset requirements rather than from a fixed density preset.
Lay out major forms and deformation loops first. Give shoulders, hips, elbows, knees and facial openings enough structure for their actual range of motion; keep poles away from heavily bending areas.
Use snapping or a projection modifier deliberately and inspect the surface from multiple angles. Check that points have not jumped to the far side of a thin shell or bridged separate pieces.

Control edge spacing and density by silhouette and deformation importance. Remove internal faces, accidental duplicates, non-manifold boundaries and tiny slivers where they violate the intended surface.
Compare the low mesh with the sculpt under neutral lighting and at the intended distance. Preserve recognisable proportions before spending the remaining budget on small detail.
Create UVs and a diagnostic normal bake on a separate copy; fix projection and smoothing problems before final texture work.

Triangulate an export copy and test representative bends or facial poses on the actual rig. Inspect weights and volume after triangulation rather than assuming a clean static wireframe will deform well.
Deliver the sculpt, editable retopology, export mesh and observed counts separately. Name unresolved deformation or target import checks instead of claiming universal topology quality.

blender-gltf-export.name: Blender Gltf Export

blender-gltf-export.whenToUse: Deliver a reproducible glTF or GLB with verified transforms, materials and animation.
steps: Inspect the installed exporter and target renderer versions, intended objects, units, axes, pivots, materials and animation clips. Keep a source blend file and use a dedicated export collection or explicit selection.

Choose GLB for a packed deliverable or a separate glTF package when its companion files are required. Collect the complete dependency set; a glTF JSON file alone may not contain its buffers or textures.
Check the target material and supported extensions. Resolve unsupported shader-node behavior through an intentional bake or compatible material, and keep a record of any visual approximation.

Inspect animation export modes against the installed version, including action slots and NLA organization. Verify the actual selected actions; do not assume historical exporter options still group clips identically.

Export to a deterministic project path without overwriting unrelated assets, then load the file through a validator or the target importer. Read actual errors rather than treating a successful file write as import success.

Compare scale, orientation, bounds, material channels, textures, deformation and clip timing in the real destination. Check missing dependencies and resource budgets at the intended gameplay distance.
Deliver the source, export package and exact tested importer/runtime details. Keep compression or animation-pointer extensions conditional on verified target support.

figma-prototyping.name: Figma Prototyping
figma-prototyping.description: Build and exercise coherent prototype flows using only advertised Figma capabilities.
figma-prototyping.whenToUse: Build and exercise coherent prototype flows using only advertised Figma capabilities.
steps: Inspect the file, page, reusable components, device sizes and advertised write/prototype operations. Identify the entry flow, success state, recoverable failures and the user action each transition represents.

Make a state map before adding interactions: loading, empty, error, disabled, back, close and cancellation where relevant. Reuse current tokens and real content so the prototype matches the product architecture.
Build or reuse the smallest set of component states and screens required for the flow. Preserve naming and stable component properties; do not detach shared instances merely to change one label.
When the account and live tools support them, use typed variables and explicit actions for state changes. Keep names and initial values understandable and avoid impossible combinations of state.

Wire transitions only through actual supported operations. If the connected plugin cannot author prototype links, create clearly annotated editable states and an interaction specification; do not claim the prototype is runnable.
Exercise the real prototype from its starting frame with representative mouse/touch actions. Test repeated opens, back navigation, reset behavior, long content and the failure path.
Check that destinations, overlays and feedback preserve context. Verify keyboard behavior only when the actual runtime allows that test; do not infer accessibility from frame appearance.
Keep the editable file and list observed working flows, implementation-only annotations and unresolved host limitations. A static screenshot is not evidence of functional interactions.

canvas-svg-ui.name: Canvas Svg Ui
canvas-svg-ui.description: Create editable SVG interface assets that import and render consistently.
steps: Inspect the target dimensions, existing style tokens, intended UI role and destination renderer. Decide whether the request calls for a static SVG artifact or native interactive controls; SVG artwork alone does not implement application behavior.

Use a coherent viewBox, predictable coordinates and consistent spacing, strokes and optical weight. Group related objects with meaningful names and keep important content inside the intended safe bounds.

Prefer portable vector shapes and verified embedded assets. Avoid script, event-handler attributes, unexpected external resources and unsupported filters; inspect the destination capability before relying on advanced effects.

Preserve editable text when the destination has the required fonts, or provide an intentional portable alternative and retain the original editable source. Check actual wrapping, glyph support and long labels.

Build representative component states and label their intended behavior. Wire real actions only in a connected native application or code runtime, using that runtime’s controls and accessibility model.

Render the SVG at small, target and enlarged sizes; inspect clipping, missing images, contrast and thin details. Check whether strokes scale as intended and preserve transparent backgrounds when requested.
Import the actual artifact into the destination when available and read its resulting structure or render. A local file path is an artifact location, not an uploaded engine asset ID.
Deliver the editable SVG and any required dependencies with real render/import evidence. Report unsupported typography or interactions instead of flattening them silently.
